records.title: British applied psychology of subnormality
JaimedeMeloand ArvindPanagariya, Eds.,New Dimensions in Regional IntegrationCambridge, UK and New York: Cambridge Univ. Press, 1993; paperback edition 1995. xxviii + 473 pp., incl. index.
Anti-Embolism Stockings and Heel Sores in Paraplegics
records.abstract: This dataset contains multiple measures of psychological processes that have previously been found to vary cross-culturally: individualism, collectivism, closeness to others, attributional style, object categorisation, drawing style and self-enhancement. Respondents are all residents of East London, with most falling into three main groups: first generation British Bangladeshis, second generation British Bangladeshis, and non-migrants with no Bangladeshi or South Asian heritage. The data also contains various demographic and lifestyle measures, such as education level, family contact, mass media use, age, and age of migration (for first generation migrants). Please see attached publication (Mesoudi, Magid & Hussain, 2016, PLOS ONE) for more details. Until recently, psychologists assumed that people from different societies all think in the same way as we do in the West - that there is a universal human psychology shared by everyone on the planet. However, when psychologists started testing non-Western people, rather than the American and British undergraduates who typically do psychology experiments, they found intriguing cultural differences. For example, there are differences in perception: Westerners focus on single objects, whereas non-Westerners focus on the relationships between objects. If you show a British and a Japanese person a scene containing lots of objects, the British person is subsequently better at recognising the objects if they are presented on their own, whereas the Japanese person has better memory if the object is presented in the original scene. Or differences in explaining other people's behaviour: Westerners explain behaviour of others in terms of fixed personality traits, whereas non-Westerners explain actions in terms of social contexts. A British teacher might explain a student's poor exam performance in terms of their laziness or lack of intelligence, whereas a Korean teacher might appeal instead to the overbearing pressure to succeed academically. But why do people from different cultures think differently? This is the central question addressed by this project. Several explanations are possible: it could be that psychological variation is caused by genetic differences between populations, and cognitive style is inherited genetically from parents. Alternatively, parents could have a non-genetic influence, through direct teaching or passive observation. Or psychological traits could be transmitted non-parentally, via peers, formal schooling, or the mass media. We will take advantage of a unique natural experiment to tease apart these factors: immigration. If the UK-born children of non-Western immigrants resemble their parents in their psychological traits, we can infer that those traits are transmitted from parents either genetically or culturally. If, on the other hand, they resemble local non-immigrants, then non-parental influence must be at work. We will then see whether this shift is associated with specific factors, such as years of schooling, exposure to mass media, or bilingualism. Another way of explaining psychological variation is in terms of history. For example, it has been suggested that Western individualism arose in ancient Greece as a response to solitary herding, whereas Eastern collectivism arose in ancient China as a response to collective rice farming. We will test this by simulating these conditions in the lab, as an experimental "microcosm" of cultural history, to see whether solitary action stimulates individualism and collective action stimulates collectivism. Finally, we will develop a web app that will let us test these ideas in multiple countries, beyond the UK, and specifically targeting immigrant groups. If these relationships hold across several regions, we can be more confident that they are valid. On the other hand, differences between regions might also be valuable. If immigrants acculturate faster in London than elsewhere, as suggested by pilot data, we can identify why this is, such as differences in mass media influence, bilingualism or family size. This project has major potential benefits for the successful integration of immigrants to the UK. Psychological differences can constitute a barrier to successful social and economic integration. For example, non-Western students can find it difficult to cope in Western educational systems that favour autonomy and creative thinking. Knowing the origin of these differences can help to overcome them better, for example by targeting parents (if parents have an influence) or the media (if the media plays a role).

records.title: The History Augmented Solow Model
Fertility, the Quality of Children and Economic Growth
records.abstract: This paper develops a theory of the fertility choice that focus on the shadow price of the quality of children and fertility rate within a framework of long term economic growth.The analysis also links the shadow price of quality with the interaction between fertility and economic growth.Through the choice of per child quality within family, the analysis contributes to narrowing the many remaining gaps between endogenous family decisions on fertility and aggregate economic growth.

records.title: Contributions of agricultural economics to critical policy issues: selected papers presented at the XXVI IAAE conference
records.abstract: Agricultural economists are well aware of the many demands by policy makers and the wider society for improving the basic conditions of food security, poverty reduction, clean environment, and efficient, if not fair, trade. Traditional research issues related to production efficiency and technology adoption have, therefore, gradually been broadened to include several new topics in the research agenda, addressing questions of food safety, supply chain integration, water scarcity and biodiversity management, migration, and the nonfarm economy. The conference program for the 26th Conference of the International Association of Agricultural Economics (IAAE) provided a wide opportunity for scholars to present their research findings and to enter into debate with peers and policy makers. The conference took place in Gold Coast (Australia) and assembled more than 1,000 attendants during the week of 12–18 August 2006. The conference committee was extremely pleased to receive almost 850 contributed papers and after thorough review a total of 358 papers were selected, of which eventually 320 were presented in 72 panel sessions.1 A particular effort was made to structure the paper presentations along a number of thematic lines, thus enabling the participants to discuss related issues and compare the research methodologies applied to similar questions. Another important consideration was to define tracks throughout the program. Thus, six critical policy issues emerged as major areas of concern to researchers: Poverty and Food Security (41 papers), Markets and Institutions (70 papers), Technical Change in Agriculture (49 papers), Environment and Development (58 papers), Consumers and Supply Chains (57 papers), and Trade and Integration (46 papers). The first two issues focus on the prospects for reducing hunger and poverty, either through targeted support measures or by improving poor peoples' access to factor markets and institutions. The next two issues address different options for improving resource use efficiency and environmental sustainability in agricultural production. Finally, the last two issues deal with commodity markets and exchange, trade regulations, and the functioning of (inter)national value chains. We will discuss briefly the most important demands to the profession that are relevant in each of these policy areas, followed by an overview of recent contributions from research to address these issues. Main attention is given to the identification of new topics and/or innovative analytical approaches that were presented during the conference.2 The selected papers included in this special issue provide an adequate illustration of the progress in our professional field in each of the thematic fields and can thus be considered as outstanding pieces of research that deserve our full attention. Problems of (rural) poverty and food security have always received major attention in agricultural economics. The fundamental role of the agricultural sector in providing food to the growing urban population during the transition process of the economy, and the possibilities for improving agricultural productivity (per unit of land and labor) represent classical—albeit still highly relevant—research issues (Johnston and Mellor, 1961; Schultz, 1964; Timmer, 2002). Food security is increasingly addressed from the demand side, paying attention to rural employment and purchasing power as key determinants for getting access to food. Consequently, rural poverty should also be considered in relation to the imperfect functioning of factor and commodity markets and the prevailing constraints in the institutional setting (see also Section 3), thus giving rise to a more complete understanding of the structural causes of chronic poverty and food insecurity (Pingali, 2006). During the last decade, the discussion on rural poverty has been substantially broadened, paying attention to the options for nonfarm and off-farm employment and (inter)national migration as potential pathways out of poverty (Haggblade et al., 2002). The classical debate regarding the future of smallholder farms thus became more oriented toward so-called outside options (Lipton, 2005). Whereas the importance of labor market engagement is now generally acknowledged, it became also clear that this may give rise to large socioeconomic differentiation and new inequalities (Reardon et al., 1992). China is a critical case in this respect, facing rapidly increasing income gaps between rural and urban areas. Within the framework of the Millennium Development Goals, the attention for measuring progress in poverty reduction and for identifying pockets of chronic poverty strongly increased. The growing availability of detailed data sets for poverty measurement—made available from the country-wide Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers—encouraged new research regarding intertemporal poverty dynamics, spatial poverty targeting, and intrahousehold income distribution. In addition, innovative analytical tools for analyzing poverty-growth linkages at household, village, and regional level enable a better understanding of the diversity of pathways out of poverty. The three selected papers included in this special issue address poverty and food security from different angles. Arndt and Simler present a poverty analysis using endogenous absolute poverty lines with data from Mozambique, proposing a bootstrapping method for reducing the impact of sampling errors on poverty measures. They consistently demonstrate that this procedure, accounting for specified differences in poverty across geographical domains, has many advantages compared to traditional approaches. Yamano analyzes the long-term economic impacts of orphanhood mostly as a result of the AIDS epidemic, examining the education attainment and land inheritance of former orphans, who have lost at least one parent before reaching the age of 15 years, using household survey data from Kenya. The paper finds clear indications of lower educational attainment among former maternal orphans, but no significant difference in land inheritance. Finally, Kuiper and Ruben provide a stylized microsimulation model with material from a remote village in Northern Ethiopia to analyze the role of heterogeneous household assets in policies aiming at poverty reduction, indicating the implications for within-village income inequality and soil erosion. Three sets of policies are explored: technology improvement, infrastructure investment, and off-farm employment through migration or cash for work programs. While single policy instruments could reduce poverty headcount but frequently increase income inequality, combining market and employment policies assists poorer households better to overcome their asset limitations. Reducing the reliance of households on agriculture offers a win-win situation of reducing poverty and maintaining natural resources. Combining policies thus may be helpful to overcome asset limitations, to target policies to the poorest households and to reduce income inequalities. Market and institutional reforms are increasingly considered as a key element in policy strategies toward economic participation and sustainable growth. In many developing countries, structural adjustment programs (SAP) that started in the 1980s were intended to reduce market failures and to eliminate the traditional urban bias (Krueger, 1992). In a similar vein, reforms in property rights regimes (i.e., land titling) and privatization of former state services were meant to accompany a more market-based development. However, given the fact that rural markets in developing countries are rather thin and that barriers to entry tend to prevent real competition, results of the SAPs proved to be rather ambiguous (Badiane, 2000). Recent progress in thinking about the nature of rural markets and the endogenous character of agrarian institutions (Binswanger, 2006) gives room to new research concerning the role of transaction costs, risk management, and property rights regimes in economic development. Attention is therefore given to options for strengthening institutional relations and collective action between rural agents (including public–private partnerships) and strategies for managing price variability over time and space (Gilbert, 1998). Earlier analyses regarding the operations of factor markets for land, labor, and finance markets (Binswanger et al., 1994) are extended to adequately address market interlinkages, while strategies for improved commodity market integration and supply chain management are launched to improve price transmission and bargaining power (see also Section 6). The three selected papers that deal with rural markets and institutions provide a good illustration of current progress in research. The paper by Fort analyzes the impact of changes in asset inequality on economic growth, using a time-variant measure for land distribution with a panel database that includes observations for more than 30 countries over three decades. A system GMM estimator is used to generate unbiased and consistent regression estimates. The study finds robust and significant negative signs for land inequality in the growth regressions, indicating that changes in asset distribution are an important factor in economic development. Differences in property rights regimes and education prove to be critical to guarantee adequate transmission. Brosig et al. analyze the dynamics of labor market participation of Chinese rural households. Based on a farm household framework, the choice between four distinct labor market participation states is empirically analyzed. A discrete time hazard approach is used to analyze households' labor market participation histories, particularly the movements between autarky and participation and the shifts between part- and full-time farming. Results suggest a decreasing risk of moving from one regime to another with an increasing time a household resides in one of these states. Furthermore, the likelihood of starting any participation in labor markets and to start part-time farming are considerably higher than to end participation or to return to full-time farming. Kassie and Holden analyze the efficiency of sharecropping systems in Ethiopia, comparing the traditional model of the Marshallian inefficiency with threats of eviction hypotheses that have opposite effects on land productivity of sharecropped plots. Empirical results were consistent with the latter hypothesis, finding higher land productivity on sharecropped plots than on share tenants' own plots, and higher land productivity on sharecropped plots of nonkin than compared to kin tenants. The data analysis allows controls for unobservable household characteristics and for observable plot characteristics. First-order stochastic dominance analysis indicates that sharecropped plots' yield distribution clearly dominated the yield distribution from share tenants' own plots, whereas nonkin sharecropped plots' output value distribution also dominated the output value distribution from kin sharecrop plots. Research on improved and more efficient production technologies for cropping and livestock activities belongs to the core of the agricultural economics profession. Based on extensive field surveys among representative farmers, sound conclusions can be drawn regarding optimal input allocation and output mix under given market conditions (Ali and Byerlee, 1991; Battese, 1992). In addition, many research efforts have been devoted to a better understanding of adoption behavior, considering farm size, education, and market linkages as critical farm household characteristics (Feder et al., 1985). Finally, considerable evidence has been raised to establish the rate of returns to different types of investments in agricultural R&D (Alston et al., 1995) Analytical procedures for a sound analysis of technical change in agriculture are nowadays well established. Partial approaches have been replaced by whole-farm analysis, and frontier techniques are commonly used to identify the yield gap. In addition to mathematical programming methods, econometric and (non)parametric techniques are widely applied to detect underlying causes of yield differences (Coelli, 1995). Dynamic efficiency studies relying on panel data are increasingly used to decompose efficiency differences. New study areas related to issues of biotechnology adoption, integrated pest and nutrient management, and organic farming are addressed with similar techniques. The debate on the role of technology for agricultural and rural development has been gradually shifting in recent years, devoting more attention to (i) aspects of risk management as a key condition for smallholder adoption, (ii) the adaptation of farming systems to major climatic challenges (see Section 5), and (iii) the implications of market linkages for dovetailing farmers' production decisions to consumer demands (see Section 6). The conference papers selected for inclusion in this special issue provide adequate state-of-the-art research regarding the role of technology change. Börner et al. analyze the impact of rainfall and price variability on rangeland management decisions in the South African savanna region. Using stochastic and deterministic simulation models, their results indicate that price policies only have a limited impact for reducing bush encroachment, whereas better timing of animal sales and purchases would yield more pronounced utility effects. Also more effective technologies for fire control are promising measures to encourage sustainable rangeland management. The paper by Diagne and Demont takes a new look at empirical adoption models, providing a detailed analysis of the differences in technology adoption between a treatment and a control group, using propensity score matching to control for unobserved differences. Data from rice farmers in Cote d'Ivoire have been used to show that the potential adoption rates of new rice varieties might have been considerably larger if exposure to new technologies would have been offered to a larger population. The interface between development and environment has been subject to much research, originating through the well-known debates on the Kuznetz curve (Grossmann and Krueger, 1995). In subsequent periods, much attention has been devoted to microeconomic options for reducing environmental externalities, and macroeconomic policies for balancing production and environmental concerns. Recent studies are especially concerned with the management of limited water and energy resources and the remaining biodiversity at local and regional level, and with the implications of carbon and greenhouse gas emissions for climate change at global and local level. Agricultural policies for the environment are also considering new instruments, ranging from public taxation to payments for environmental services. While in Western countries options for rewarding multifunctional agriculture are introduced, in many developing countries (inter)national compensation payments still scarcely reach primary producers. The implementation of efficient and equitable regimes for water tariffs, biodiversity control, and carbon payments still meets numerous institutional constraints related to monitoring, enforcement, and control (Baland et al., 2007). Analytical methods for addressing environmental concerns in agricultural economics are developing rapidly. Starting with traditional cost-benefit analysis, most recent studies now apply some kind of integrated bioeconomic approach that accounts for feedback mechanisms. In addition, regional (watershed) models that include spatial distribution effects are increasingly used.
