records.title: Violent conflict and the child quantity-quality trade-off
records.abstract: This paper estimates the effect of childcare availability on parents’ employment probability using the timing of the grandmothers’ death– the primary childcare provider in Mexico– as identifying variation. I use a triple-difference to disentangle the effect of coinhabiting grandmothers’ deaths due to their impact on childcare from their effects due to alternative mechanisms. Through their impact on childcare availability, grandmothers’ deaths reduce mothers’ employment rate by 12 percentage points (27 percent) and do not affect fathers’ employment rate. The negative effect on mothers’ employment is smaller where public daycare is more available, or private daycare or schools are more affordable.

records.title: Maternal genetic risk for depression and child human capital
records.abstract: We here address the causal relationship between the maternal genetic risk for depression and child human capital using UK birth-cohort data. We find that an increase of one standard deviation (SD) in the maternal polygenic risk score for depression reduces their children's cognitive and non-cognitive skill scores by 5 to 7% of a SD throughout adolescence. Our results are robust to a battery of sensitivity tests addressing, among others, concerns about pleiotropy and dynastic effects. Our Gelbach decomposition analysis suggests that the strongest mediator is genetic nurture (through maternal depression itself), with genetic inheritance playing only a marginal role.

records.title: Concentration of Reproduction in Austria: General Trends and Differentials by Educational Atteinment and Urban-Rural Setting
records.venue: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
records.abstract: In this paper, we explore the inter-individual diversity in fertility among women in Austria for the female birth cohorts 1917-1961. Comparative studies revealed that all Western countries have witnessed a decline in the concentration of reproduction during the 20th century, a trend that has reversed for the most recent cohorts which have reached the end of their reproductive period. This reversal, mainly triggered by an increase in childlessness, has been hardly perceptible in Austria and limited to urban municipalities. Changes in fertility and concentration have followed very different trajectories by educational attainment as well as by the type of municipality in which women lived at age 15. Within educational categories, we found large differentials by profession and intergenerational educational mobility. A consequence of the concentration of reproduction is that the level of cohort fertility differs from the average sibship size seen from the children’s perspective. In the Austrian case, in contrast to the pronounced fertility differentials by educational attainment, the average sibship size experienced by children became almost independent of parents’ education. In contrast to the negative correlation between fertility and concentration found in earlier studies for the first demographic transition and the baby boom, the fertility level and concentration moved in the same direction, and did so for an extended time period following the baby boom, accelerating changes from the children’s perspective.

records.title: On the Identification of Tertiary Education Expansion Effect on Fertility
Responsiveness of Child Health to Maternal Fertility in Central African Republic
records.abstract: This paper investigates the effect of fertility on child health status, using data from the sixth edition of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS6) of the Central African Republic (CAR) collected in 2018 by the government’s statistics office. Specifically, the paper seeks: to assess the direct and indirect effects of maternal fertility on child health. To achieve these objectives, we use a framework based on the quantity-quality theory of the new household economy and the control function modeling strategy—which simultaneously corrects for endogeneity, sample selectivity and unobserved heterogeneity biases. Results show that, having an additional child significantly increases the risk of sickness in children under 5 years in CAR. Results also show a positive and highly significant indirect effect of fertility on sickness as depicted by the interaction of fertility and its residual—a clear indication of undesirable complementarities between fertility and unobserved correlates of fertility in widening sickness probability among children. These findings suggest that public intervention that improves spending on social services, such as education, preventive child health and family planning programmes, would reduce fertility, and initiate the process of better child health and productivity in adulthood.

records.title: The Effect of Trade Liberalization on Marriage and Fertility: Evidence from Indian Census
Toward a Socio-Economic Theory
records.abstract: A socio-economic system will be viewed as a dynamical system which assigns to each family or consumer unit various quantities of economic goods, factors of production, and family size depending upon last periods quantities. Since the populated world is a cylinder, prosperity eventually returns to any former location with the establishment of a new social system and a consequent decay. Strictly interpreted, the theory says that the socio-economic system is cyclic, at least in some of its components. Less strictly interpreted, the socio-economic system is recurrent. For application to a socio-economic system, one must verify the continuity properties. Important institutions enforcing the Protestant ethic are compulsory education, social security and medicare, and laws whereby debts apply only to the physical estate and not to the raw labor and human capital of descendents.

records.title: Application of Artificial Intelligence and IOT for Increasing Productivity of Agricultural Sector
records.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
records.abstract: Agriculture is the major sector that feeds the ever-growing population in the world. As the population is increasing day by day globally increased food demand will be faced. Thus, agricultural productivity should be increased in a robust way. In the environment, the next green evolution has the approaches related to health of the plants, productivity and growth. By understanding the mechanism of agricultural productivity by the farmers requires automation in every stage of farming. The sustainability and productivity in forms can be expanded through technologies. Emerging strategies for improving the activity and survival of the crops can be enhanced from the seedling stage till harvesting. Through Internet of Things and artificial intelligence productivity in agriculture can increased by automated process in crop production for assessment of seed and crop qualities, diagnosing the diseases, automated irrigation system, alarm system for pesticide and fertiliser application, analysing soil fertility and erosion and applying precision farming using robotic and drone systems. By maintaining the crops at the right time major losses of crops can be reduced as well as the reduction of cost. The scope of the study for analysing the application of IOT and artificial intelligence through the proposed crop maintenance model for increasing productivity in agriculture sector.

records.title: The Heterogeneous Effect of Parental Investment on Old-Age Support: Only Children As the Main Caregivers in China
records.abstract: In an era of rapid aging and shrinking family sizes, only children have gradually become the main providers of old-age support. China offers a unique opportunity to investigate old-age support provision in one-child families due to its strict family planning policies. Using four-wave panel data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, we ask whether old-age support in one-child families is more or less motivated by parental investments than in multi-child families. Results show a coexistence of fairness maintenance thesis and singleton compensation thesis: children’s returns to parents in one-child families are weakly motivated by their parents’ large-sum investments, but strongly motivated by parental daily transfers. In one-child families, sons are more obliged to provide old-age support in return for parental transfers than are daughters. The policy implications for old-age support provision in an aging society with a declining family size are also discussed.

records.title: Quantity-Quality Trade-Off in Northeast China During the Qing Dynasty
Controlled bush harvesting as a means for restoring soil of encroached savannahs in Southern Africa
records.first_author: José María García de Castro Barragán
records.abstract: Rangelands in Namibia have experienced a shift from herbaceous to woody plant dominance which has reduced indigenous plant and animal biodiversity. It is also altering ecosystem function, and threatening subsistence pastoralism. A common approach to reduce these negative impacts is bush thinning. It is expected that removal of brushes will favorite the development of grasslands with a positive impact on their soil organic matter (SOM) stocks. On the other hand, harvesting bush from those systems removes not only biomass but also nutrients that are stored in it. Such losses can decrease soil fertility which is likely to affect the soil carbon stocks on a long term. In search of a better understanding of the consequences of such a restoration approach, the objective of the present work is to study the impact of bush removal on the quantity, quality and biochemical recalcitrance of SOM as well as nutrient contents in soils of an encroached savannah which was subjected to bush harvesting. Therefore, we sampled a chronosequence of soils with up to fifteen years after bush thinning. Their SOM was characterized by solid-state NMR spectroscopy and composition was related to its biochemical recalcitrance determined by measuring the CO2 evolution during microbial degradation in a microcosms experiment of 3 months. First results indicate that up to two years after bush harvesting SOM contents of the soil were decreased, although a recovery was observed with increasing time after harvesting. Ongoing analysis of the stable isotopic ratios are performed to identify if this dynamic is caused by lower litter input due to the change of vegetation from bush to grass or by a faster turnover of the SOM, induced by alteration of the environmental conditions due to bush removal (light, soil moisture, temperature etc.). Acknowledgement: The authors would like to express their gratitude to the European Commission for the financial support of this research within the European Framework Programme for Research and Innovation Horizon 2020 (Grant No. 101036401).

records.title: Declining Quantity and Quality of Births in Chile amidst the COVID‐19 Pandemic
records.abstract: Abstract Extensive demographic scholarship shows that the population‐level implications of mortality crises such as the COVID‐19 pandemic extend beyond mortality dynamics to affect fertility and family‐formation strategies. Using novel municipality‐level data from Chile covering all births that occurred between January 2017 and December 2021, this study explores trends in fertility and implications of the COVID‐19 pandemic for “quantum” and “quality” of births in the Chilean context. Building both a monthly and a yearly panel of 346 municipalities and leveraging fixed‐effects regression analyses, we focus on births and crude birth rates to measure quantum, while quality is assessed through the share of births that are low‐weight (LBW) and preterm (PTB). Our findings provide evidence of a significant drop in fertility in the wake of COVID—of the magnitude of a reduction of 1.3 live births per 1,000 individuals—which reaches a minimum around February 2021, followed by an incipient rebound in late 2021. Moreover, estimates on child health at birth suggest that the COVID period was associated with an increase in LBW and, foremost, PTB, by 1 and 2.2 percentage points, respectively. Findings from this study shed light on the role of policy interventions in the health arena and the linkages between short‐ and long‐run effects in relation to the various COVID‐19 waves in Chile.

records.title: The effects of trade liberalization on gender inequality in central america and its relevance to the textile and apparel industry and academy
records.abstract: [EMBARGOED UNTIL 5/1/2023] Addressing gender (in)equality issues is a concern in Central America (CA) and a global challenge as measured by the Gender Inequality Index (GII). This study used the Heckscher-Ohlin (1933) theory of international trade and the Becker (2010) theory of economic discrimination to examine the impact of CAFTA-DR and TA trade on gender (in)equality in CA. To achieve this purpose, the study used a mixed-methods research design and had two specific questions: (a) RQ1 - "is the implementation of CAFTA-DR and growth in textile and clothing exports and imports associated with gender (in)equality in CAFTA-DR countries? and (b) RQ2 - "how do textile and apparel manufacturing industry women professionals and academics in El Salvador perceive the changes in gender (in)equality overtime due to CAFTA-DR's implementation". The findings suggests that the implementation of CAFTA-DR is associated with positive changes in four out of the five areas of gender (in)equality, including maternal mortality rate, adolescent birth rate, women in parliament seats, and labor force participation of women. The findings also suggest that changes in TA import and exports have had varying degrees of positive effect on gender (in)equality across CAFTA-DR countries and across all GII dimensions. Qualitatively, this study found that more women in El Salvador were pursued careers in the TA industry and collaborated with peers to learn the foundational techniques. CAFTA-DR. Overall, the findings supported Heckscher-Ohlin theory of international trade (1933) and Becker's (1957) economic discrimination theory which suggests, as countries develop and trade grows, gender disparities improve overtime. From the findings, scholars might assess how to improve the lives of women working in TA industries by researching how to close the gaps on (in)equality that impact their at-work and at-home lives as the industry continues to grow and develop.

Investment in Children's Human Capital Through PAYG Pension Systems
records.abstract: Central bank independence (CBI) has long been considered a key aspect of effective monetary policy, as it allows central banks to make decisions free from political interference. However, the global financial crisis of 2007–2008 and recent events such as the COVID-19 pandemic and armed conflict in Ukraine have threatened CBI. This article aims to examine the impact of these events on CBI in OECD member countries, both on a de jure and de facto level, using a variety of indicators. The results suggest that CBI has largely remained unchanged in most countries, but there is disturbing evidence of political interference in CBI in the Republic of Türkiye.

records.title: 'Sex in Marriage Is a Divine Gift'? Evidence on the Quantity-Quality Trade-off from the Manila Contraceptive Ban
records.abstract: We analyze the trade-off between child quantity and child quality in developing countries by estimating the effect of family size on child’s education in urban Philippines. To isolate exogenous changes in family size, we exploit a policy shock: in the late 1990s, the mayor of Manila enacted a municipal ban on modern contraceptives. Since other comparable cities in the Manila metropolitan area were not affected by the ban, this allows us to implement a difference-in-difference estimation of the effect on family size. We also exploit the fact that older mothers were less likely to become pregnant during the ban. Our results indicate that the contraceptive ban led to a significant increase in family size. They also provide evidence of a quality-quantity trade-off: increased family size led to a sizable decrease in educational attainment.

records.title: The Day the World Stopped Working
records.abstract: The title of this essay refers not, as one might have imagined, to that moment in the spring of 2020 near the beginning of the coronavirus pandemic when tens of millions of people across the world were suddenly laid off or furloughed or told to work from home and a worldwide economic slowdown began. Despite the echoes of this most recent crisis, my title refers instead to all the discourses regarding the “end of work” that have cropped up periodically since the end of the nineteenth century and that drew widespread public attention back in the 1990s, due in large part to Jeremy Rifkin's book The End of Work.1 In that now classic work of 1995, Rifkin, the well-known economic and social theorist, predicted the end of work as we know it, as more and more jobs once performed by human beings in the agricultural, manufacturing, and even the service sector become automated and taken over by machines, robots, and computers. Rifkin suggested at the time that “massive unemployment of a kind never before experienced” would be “all but inevitable in the coming decades” (Rifkin 1995, 5) as we enter into “a new phase in world history,” “one in which fewer and fewer workers [would] be needed to produce the goods and services for the global population” (Rifkin 1995, xvi).A quarter of a century later, it might appear either that Rifkin's dire prognostications were woefully misguided, since unemployment in the United States before the unexpected coronavirus outbreak was well below 4%, despite the continuing automation of so many industries, or that those predictions of increasing unemployment or underemployment and greater and greater income inequality as a result of automation were in fact beginning to be realized before the pandemic and have actually been borne out in some rather stark and unexpected ways by the pandemic (even if, as of this writing, unemployment in the United States has once again fallen below 4%).2 For there is no doubt that the current pandemic will have demonstrated just how many of the basic needs of global populations can be satisfied, at least in many parts of the developed world, with only a fraction of the workforce fully employed, and it has led even more industries (from entertainment to education) to recognize that they can best survive by automating more and more of their services or by replacing full-time workers with low-paid or part-time workers. In this second scenario, the 2019–2022 pandemic will have simply highlighted or provided a final impetus to the movement of greater and greater globalization, job loss, and massive income inequality that Rifkin predicted would transform the way we think about the nature of work itself in the twenty-first century. Indeed, as we have all come to see firsthand over the past two years, almost nothing about what we call our “workaday world” has gone unchallenged by the current crisis, not the notion of world, for which the divisions have become at once less fixed due to the flexibility offered by telework and more strictly policed by nation-states responding to the pandemic, not the notion of the day, with the postwar, Monday through Friday, 9-to-5 workday being replaced by everything from part-time or irregular gig work to the 24/7 model of work that has blurred the boundary between leisure and work and transformed living spaces into workplaces, and not, therefore, the notion of work, which is undergoing dramatic transformation as a result of the current crisis and the more structural and systemic forces related to automation.Now, as a philosopher rather than an economist, I am woefully unqualified to enter into the economic debates concerning the accuracy of Rifkin's predictions. records.title: Reducing the Teacher-Student Ratio as a Strategy for Elementary Schools in Taiwan to Response the Declining Birth Rate Crisis
records.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
records.abstract: The declining birth rate in Taiwan has become a significant concern that has affected various aspects of society, including the field of education. Elementary schools, being the earliest stage of compulsory education, have shouldered the responsibility of not only providing quality education but also facing the impact of the declining birth rate. This paper analyzes data from the Ministry of Education (MOE) and National Development Council to discuss the teacher-student ratio in elementary school education in Taiwan and provides suggestions for the current and future situation. The annual enrollment of elementary schools has been declining since 2000 but showed a temporary upward trend from 2016 to 2018 before facing a rapid decline from 2021 to 2028. The number of teachers has also increased slightly, but the number and distribution of teachers will be crucial, especially during the upcoming period of declining enrollment. The average number of students per class in elementary schools has been around 23, and the teacher-student ratio has slightly decreased from 2016 to 2021, suggesting that elementary schools in Taiwan have the conditions to reduce the teacher-student ratio, which could be beneficial for education. Therefore, actively reducing the teacher-student ratio could be a strategy for elementary schools in Taiwan to address the challenges posed by the declining birth rate.

records.title: Twin birth rates and obstetric interventions in Iceland: A nationwide study from 1997 to 2018
records.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Twin pregnancies are associated with increased antepartum and intrapartum risks. Limited multiple embryo transfers are associated with decreased twin birth rates. We aimed to study the effect of 2009 Icelandic regulations on twin birth rates and examine obstetric intervention rates for twin births during the study period. METHODS: The study included all births (N = 94 028) in Iceland during 1997-2018. Twin birth rates and obstetric intervention rates were compared over birth year periods using modified Poisson regression adjusted for confounders. RESULTS: An observed decrease in the twin birth rate trend was most notable from 2006 until 2009. Twin birth decreased in 2009-2013 (prevalence ratio [PR] 0.74, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.64-0.86) and in 2014-2018 (PR 0.74, 95% CI 0.64-0.86) compared with 1997-2002. This decrease was only evident for women aged 30+ years in stratified analysis. Induction of labor rates increased from 26% in 1997-2002 to 44% in 2014-2018 (adjusted rate ratio [ARR] 2.10, 95% CI 1.72-2.57) whereas elective cesarean section (ARR 0.80, 95% CI 0.59-1.07) and urgent cesarean section (ARR 0.79, 95% CI 0.63-1.00) rates appeared to decline. CONCLUSION: Twin births decreased during the study period. International guidelines published before the Icelandic regulations may have affected twin birth rates in Iceland. Induction of labor rates for twins increased while cesarean section rates decreased.

records.abstract: This study shows that the new pension program in the People’s Republic of China can fundamentally alter the traditional support system between generations. While it lessens the role of working-age adults to provide support to their old-age parents, it may also have an impact on the educational investment of parents in their children depending on their gender. Along with the new pension program, policies to reduce school dropout and to support children who receive less parental investment may mitigate the unintended adverse impact.

records.title: Essays on the Economics of Health and Education
records.abstract: This dissertation consists of three chapters on the economics of health and education. In Chapter 2, I examine the effect of prenatal exposure to Agent Orange, a dioxin- contaminated herbicide that was dispersed on a large scale in South Vietnam for military operations during the Vietnam War, on educational attainment of Vietnamese civilians. The identification strategy exploits province-by-cohort variation in the intensity of Agent Orange sprayed. I find that controlling for conventional bombing, cohorts exposed in utero to Agent Orange (who were born between 1962 and 1971) have lower educational attainment compared to other birth cohorts. The same inference is obtained when employing an instrumental-variable approach that uses the density of North Vietnamese army bases as an instrument for the intensity of Agent Orange. The results demonstrate that prenatal exposure to toxic chemicals has a long-lasting detrimental effect on human capital formation. Chapter 3 investigates the impact of maternal education on child mortality. The government of Peru amended its constitution to increase compulsory education from six to eleven years in 1993. This constitutional amendment provides a natural experiment to investigate the impact of maternal education on child mortality. Exploiting differences in the reform exposure by age, I find that mothers who were exposed to the reform were less likely to experience the death of a child. There is also evidence that the reform caused a decline in infant mortality. These results are not driven by the age difference between mothers who were treated by the reform and those who were not treated. Additional analyses reveal that the reform increased age at first birth, decreased desired fertility, reduced smoking, and improved economic opportunities for women. The results demonstrate that compulsory schooling may be a useful policy tool to improve women’s education, which can, in turn, enhance the survival of their children. In Chapter 4, I explore the effect of education on women’s empowerment. The government of Uganda introduced an education reform that eliminated school fees for primary school-age children in 1997. I find that an increase in education, generated by the reform, has a positive impact on women’s empowerment. Specifically, an increase in schooling, due to the reform, improves women’s involvement in decision making within the household by increasing their likelihood of having a final say on issues related to their own health, about large household expenses, and regarding visits to family or relatives. records.title: The determinants of the timing of first marriage for women in Taiwan.
records.abstract: The objective of this study is to investigate the effects of parental family, socialization and premarital work on women's marital timing in Taiwan. The variables associated with parental family include income, durable goods, availability of parents, availability of married siblings, sibship size, and birth position. The variables related to socialization are education, birthplace, and urban experience. Variables associated with work are employment status, length of nonfamilial employment, work hours, job income, and job satisfaction. Data for this study come from a two-wave panel survey of young women in Taiwan. The first wave of interviews was conducted in 1971 among both married and single women aged 18-29. The 1971 interview, plus a follow-up data collection in 1978, provide marital status and marital timing through 1978. The study shows that marriage rates have declined over time and that women with urban residential experience, higher educational attainment, better parental family economic status, more older sisters, and longer nonfamilial employment tend to have lower rates of marriage. Oldest sisters also tend to get married earlier than later-born sisters. Education, however, is the most powerful determinant of marital timing. The effects of birth cohort, birthplace, birth position and parental family economic status on marital timing operate at least partially through education. The effects of education and birthplace on marriage rates have increased over time. However, the availability of parents, job income, weekly working hours and job satisfaction are unrelated with marital timing in Taiwan.

records.abstract: In daily life, the role of agriculture is crucial.The population is growing rapidly, and with it, is the need for food and work.Farmers employed conventional techniques, but they were unable to meet these demands.As a result, new automated techniques were introduced.These innovative techniques supplied the world's food needs while simultaneously creating jobs for billions of people.With the help of artificial intelligence (AI), agriculture has drastically reformed.This technique has safeguarded crop yields from a variety of conditions including climate change, population increase, job troubles, and food security concerns.The purpose of this literature review research is to examine the different uses of artificial intelligence in agricultural, such as irrigation, weeding and spraying, using sensors and other techniques implanted in robots and drones.These technologies reduce the use of water, pesticides and herbicides, preserve soil fertility and aid in the effective use of labour to increase production and quality.This report analyses the work of several scholars in order to provide a concise summary of the present state of automation in agriculture.

records.title: The mechanism of assortative mating for educational attainment: a study of Finnish and Dutch twins and their spouses
records.abstract: Introduction: Assortative mating refers describes a phenomenon in which individuals with similar phenotypic traits are more likely to mate and reproduce with each other; i.e. assortative mating occurs when individuals choose partners based on their similarity or dissimilarity in certain traits.to patterns of non-random mating of spouses leading to phenotypic resemblance. There are various theories about the its underlying mechanisms, which have different genetic consequences. Methods: We analyzed examined two possible mechanisms underlying assortative mating – phenotypic assortment and social homogamy – for educational attainment in two countries utilizing data of mono- and dizygotic twins and their spouses (1,451 Finnish and 1,616 Dutch twin-spouse pairs). Results: The spousal correlations were 0.51 in Finland and 0.45 in the Netherlands, to which phenotypic assortment contributed 0.35 and 0.30, and social homogamy 0.16 and 0.15, respectively. Conclusion: Both social homogamy and phenotypic assortment are important processes in spouse selection in Finland and the Netherlands. In both countries, phenotypic assortment contributes to a greater degree to the similarity of spouses than social homogamy.

records.title: The Journey of Humanity by Oded Galor: A Review Essay
records.abstract: The laws of history have nothing in common with a pedantic schematism. (28) Unified growth theory captures the journey of humanity over the entire course of history since the emergence of Homo Sapiens in Africa 500,000 years ago. It identifies and traces the forces that governed the process of development during the Malthusian epoch, eventually triggering the phase transition in which the human species escaped from this poverty trap into an era of sustained growth. The insights are essential for understanding the growth process in its entirety, the hurdles faced by poorer economies today in their transition from stagnation to growth, the origins of the great divergence in the wealth of nations in the past centuries, and the fingerprints of the ancient past in the fate of nations. (45) As such, The Journey of Humanity joins such celebrated large-scale histories of human development as Guns, Germs, and Steel (1997) by Jared Diamond and Why Nations Fail (2012) by Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson. It is arguably more ambitious than either with respect to the breadth of history it attempts to present and interpret. In this essay, I assess The Journey of Humanity in terms of the author's contributions to the study of growth and development; in other words, I focus on the second level at which one can read the book. First, I consider what assessment should be made about the substantive novelty in Galor's approach to understanding long-run growth dynamics—the claim that genetic diversity is a fundamental “deep root” of contemporary differences in economic development across the world. Second, I assess the overall contribution of unified growth theory beyond the set time– and context-specific theories that constitute current growth economics. I have serious reservations about Galor's arguments on the role of genetic diversity1 as well as in the value of theory of everything whose objective is to interpret the full history of human development. The conceptual framework I devised in the past few decades was inspired by insights from the mathematical field of bifurcation theory, which demonstrates how, beyond a certain threshold, minor alterations in a single factor may generate a sudden and dramatic transformation in the behaviour of complex dynamic systems. (46) For Galor (e.g., Galor and Weil 2000; Galor and Moav 2004), key bifurcations occur with respect to the evolution of technology and human capital. Incentives for families to invest in human capital depend on the state of technology in a society. This state depends initially on the size of the population, with the underlying idea that larger populations beget greater ideas. At some point, population growth sets in motion sustained growth dynamics. Why? Higher levels of population induce higher levels of technology. Higher levels of technology in turn beget more population growth, but this effect is attenuated by increased incentives on the part of parents to invest in their children's human capital. Together, one can understand transitions from a Malthusian regime as a bifurcation to a growing technology and human capital regime with population growth stabilizing to allow per capita output growth. This is the transition from a Malthusian to a post-Malthusian society. The autocatalysis of growth via the interplay of ideas and capital accumulation lies at the foundations of endogenous growth theory, in Paul Romer's Nobel Prize-winning ideas (1986, 1990) on social increasing returns to scale as well as Lucas (1988), which focuses on human capital as a source of increasing returns. Galor's contributions involve linking population growth to this process and in understanding the ways that nonlinear systems can provide insights on the quantitative properties of growth dynamics. In my judgment, this is an important new set of insights. This approach, as I have sketched out, addresses the substantive question of the dynamics of escape from the Malthusian population trap. I call this contribution methodological as it ultimately relies on features of the nonlinear systems that embed the standard substantive behavioral assumptions that link technological change, population size, and human capital investments in his framework. This is no disparagement. The history of economic development is replete with nonlinear behaviors, as is well documented in Galor (2005). Identifying which types of nonlinear models best capture the empirics of nonlinearity is enormously important. That said, it is important to understand when this class of methodological contributions enhances understanding and where it does not. There are longstanding debates in the demography literature that contrast the role of ideas and norms versus conventional economic explanations of fertility dynamics; Lesthaege and Surkyn (1988) remain an invaluable overview. These authors focus on “Western ideational change…the processes of secularization and individuation” (8) as fundamental to understanding the timing of fertility dynamics. This view is supported by many studies; Coale and Watkins (1986) is a classic on this topic, and Blanc (2022) is an interesting recent analysis providing new evidence on the role of 18th French secularization in lowering fertility. Formal models such as those Galor has developed for fertility dynamics should be understood as elucidating phenomena at a particular time and spatial scale, that is, one that implicitly aggregates across swaths of time and space and smooths out features of the phenomenon under study. This is known as coarse graining in physics and is an important tool in understanding the broad properties of systems. However, insights at one level of aggregation can mask important mechanisms at another. Abstractions and efforts to capture phenomena across wide ranges of time and space suffer the possible danger of obscuring too much by abstracting away factors in the interest of universality.2 I return to this below to the import of this cost. Galor's substantive contribution to growth theory, one that receives much attention in The Journey of Humanity, is, in contrast, problematic. It involves the claim that genetic diversity in populations is a major reason for heterogeneity in development. Ashraf and Galor (2013) are the source of this argument. The basic idea is that there exists an optimal level of genetic diversity for economic development. If diversity is too high, then trust, cooperation, and the production of public goods are inhibited. If diversity is too low, homogeneity of skills and perspectives works against creativity and innovation. The broad claim is that Europe has economically outperformed other parts of the world, in particular, Africa and indigenous populations in the Americas because it possessed a fortuitous intermediate level of diversity, while African development was inhibited by higher diversity and development in the Americas by lower diversity. They link genetic diversity to migration distance from Africa in terms of an ultimate mechanism. How do Ashraf and Galor justify this claim? Much of their evidence is derived from regressions that project levels of economic development against a statistical measure of genetic diversity. They construct year synthetic contemporary genetic diversity measures of country-specific ancestral populations based on calculations for the diversity of various ethnic groups combined with data on population flows of these groups since 1500. They further use migratory distance from Africa measures as an instrumental variable for genetic diversity to account for endogeneity of contemporary diversity as opposed to diversity with deep roots. The empirical claims of this paper can be challenged on three distinct levels. First, the paper is surprisingly mute on the marginal explanatory power of genetic diversity measures; the one calculation that appears in an online Appendix presents adjusted R2 values of 0.03 for genetic diversity and its square, which is hardly evidence of important marginal explanatory power. This matters when one considers the contribution to overall understanding of integrating genetic diversity with other growth mechanisms in a unified growth theory. Second, there is considerable reason to worry about the standard errors that are reported. Focusing on the most important regression in the paper, which uses a synthetic diversity measure in a sample of 143 countries to determine a link between genetic diversity and contemporary development, consider the reported standard errors. It takes a very heroic assumption of uncorrelatedness of the regression errors across countries to regard the standard errors associated with parameter estimates as credible.3 This is a universal problem with cross-country regressions, but it has a particular purchase here because of the paper's choices of control variables. Ashraf and Galor choose controls that are associated with other candidates for deep roots of contemporary development, such as measures of institutional quality and geography. As such they ignore higher frequency variables, such as monetary and fiscal regimes, which can exhibit correlations across countries. They have omitted a vast range of growth determinants and by implication induced complex dependences in their model errors. These theoretical considerations have been shown to matter. Kelly (2019) is a seminal analysis of unobserved spatial heterogeneity in deep roots studies. He shows that for Ashraf–Galor, there is considerable evidence of spatial heterogeneity in their 2000 per capita income regression and that correction of standard errors for this spatial correlation doubles the standard errors of the diversity parameter estimates. But note my argument is more general since the correlations in country-level errors involve more than distance. the measure of intra-population genetic diversity that we employ should be interpreted as a proxy (i.e., a correlated summary measure) for diversity amongst individuals in a myriad of observable and unobservable personal traits that may be physiological, behavioral, socially-constructed, or otherwise. (2) However, as noted by the authors of the critique, no evidence is given that the genetic diversity measure in fact proxies for those measures. The finding in this statistical model that γ ≠ 0 $\gamma \ne 0$ is treated as evidence that explanation R i ${R_i}$ constitutes one of the mechanisms underlying ω. For Galor, the R of interest is the level of genetic diversity of a country's population. Why have such regressions fallen into general disrepute? In my judgment, there are three criticisms that matter here. First, the analysis does not adequately address uncertainty in the appropriate choice of control variables in (1). For contexts such as cross-country levels of development and growth, there is no social science consensus on which additional explanations need to be included beyond those that Ashraf and Galor consider. Durlauf, Johnson, and Temple (2005) found, for economic growth, that over 140 different controls had appeared in the literature up to the time of that survey. These different controls were all, ex ante, theoretically plausible. Further, the variables were all logically compatible with each other, so that the presence of one variable did not imply that another did not have growth consequences as well.5 Ashraf and Galor investigate the robustness of their findings to “institutional, cultural, and geographical determinants of development” (37, Table 7). But as argued above, the investigation of robustness with respect to higher frequency variables is ignored except for years of schooling in a single regression (37, Table 7 Column 8). But relative to the cross-country literature, their exploration misses many candidate mechanisms and there is no basis for concluding their genetic diversity evidence is robust to choice of additional growth mechanisms. Ashraf and Galor might respond that they are estimating a reduced form of a larger system in which high-frequency variables are other endogenous variables. But this is not really an answer, for reasons suggested above. Any correlations between the deep roots and higher frequency variables are assumed to be caused by the deep roots. This is hard to justify. Why, for example, might correlations in monetary and fiscal policies between countries, which presumably have spatial aspects, have anything to do with migratory distance, another spatially correlated variable? (As an algebraic proposition, omitting a set of variables, of course, does not preserve unbiasedness of estimates of the parameters of the included variables except under orthogonality assumptions that have substantive social science content and must be argued to be credible.) It is not possible to uncover deep roots in the sense of genetic diversity or other deep roots without assumptions on the role of omitted variables in determining the phenomenon under study or the relationship between the chosen deep roots and other mechanisms. Second, regressions of form (1) assume linearity and additively separability which are functional form assumptions that do not naturally arise from the vantage point of growth and development theories. Starting with linearity, Galor's theory of genetic diversity and economic development is predicated on a nonlinear relationship between a country's development and its migratory distance from Africa, which leads Ashraf and Galor to use levels and squares of levels of genetic diversity and migratory distance to an otherwise linear regression. This omits all other types of nonlinearity. In particular, the specification used in empirical work misses nonlinearities in the dynamics themselves. By this, I mean nonlinearities in the transition function that relate GDP per capita, population levels, and the like to their past values. This is more than a debating point. As argued in Bernard and Durlauf (1996) for cross-country growth regressions and in Durlauf, Kourtellos, and Tan's (2022) for intergenerational mobility analyses, the failure to account for the full range of nonlinearity in dynamics can produce deeply misleading conclusions about the mechanisms underlying the phenomena under study. To understand the impact of this type of nonlinearity, suppose that genetic diversity had a role in setting different initial conditions pre-1500. Further, suppose it is these initial conditions that led to different long-run equilibria in output because of nonlinearities in the development process; such multiplicity is one interpretation of poverty, middle income, and affluence traps which are standard ideas in development economics. If this is the case, then contemporaneous disparities have nothing to do with diversity per se, but entirely with the initial conditions. This story is compatible with the empirical findings in Ashraf and Galor. A complementary critique occurs when interactions between growth mechanisms are assumed away by additive separability. Tan (2010) is important in demonstrating that nonlinearities in growth occur in terms of the interactions of different ultimate theories; the additive separability of (1) is not theoretically justified and, as Tan shows, may lead to misleading claims about fundamental growth determinants when interactions are ignored. Together, these arguments indicate why the robustness of the genetic diversity evidence as presented is predicated on a theoretically untenable functional form assumption. Would the claims of genetic diversity's role survive considering such alternative specifications? It is impossible to know. Third, Equation (1) assumes constant coefficients across countries. This is an imposition of a type of homogeneity concerning the marginal predictive effects of a given variable across countries. This is hard to justify for such complex, heterogeneous units. Ashraf and Galor allow for continent-level fixed effects, but it is not clear that these are adequate.6 First, why should the effects of migratory distance be constant across continents, when intercepts are not, which is the import of adding continental dummies? Second, why is the continent the correct level of aggregation for thinking about parameter heterogeneity? The Scientific7 and Industrial Revolutions did not uniformly occur across Europe. Why should there not be parameter heterogeneity at the country level as an explanation of this heterogeneity, if continent dummy variables are appropriate? Kelly (2019) again demonstrates that this matters for Ashraf and Galor. He adds dummies for the World Bank region that are finer grained than those of the original paper and finds these, in conjunction with other adjustments to assess overall robustness, can reduce parameter estimates to 30 percent of those originally reported. Important advances have been made in empirical cross-country research over the last two decades which have addressed issues of control variable uncertainty, functional forms, and parameter heterogeneity.8 With references to variable uncertainty, Fernandez, Ley, and Steel (2001), using full Bayesian methods, consider 41 candidate growth predictors and conclude that only four have posterior model inclusion probabilities higher than the prior probabilities assigned to them. Sala-i-Martin, Doppelhofer, and Miller (2004) found, using a Bayesian-frequentist hybrid method to identify robust growth determinants that, when starting with 67 candidate growth variables, only 18 appeared robustly associated with growth differences across countries. Subsequent work in growth on variable uncertainty has proven consistent with these seminal findings. Why does this matter here? The correlation structure of the errors in (1) depends on the omitted growth determinants in the equation, and variable uncertainty applies to this. With reference to nonlinearities and parameter heterogeneity, Durlauf and Johnson (1995) is an early example of an analysis that provided evidence of clubs in cross-country growth behavior. In this paper, countries with different initial incomes and literacy rates are shown to sort into different growth models, which are distinguished by different sensitivities of growth to physical and human capital accumulation. Later developments on growth clubs include Canova (2004) and Pittau, Zelli, and Johnson (2010) and demonstrate the robustness of evidence of growth clubs to different statistical formulations. This evidence undermines the class of specifications considered in Ashraf and Galor as it means their findings are those from projecting a linear model (one in which the square of genetic diversity appears as well as its level) onto observations from a nonlinear world. Thus, a range of tools is available that could have addressed the general cross-country regression problems I have described. As such Ashraf and Galor deserve criticism for failing to address the limits of cross-country growth analyses that have been shown to matter in previous work. records.title: Does parents’ cognitive ability affect household educational investment? Evidence from Chinese families with left behind children
records.abstract: The large group of left-behind children with the absence of parental accompanying are likely to have serious physical and psychological problems, which may lead to serious public safety and social economic troubles in adulthood. Such unique phenomenon calls us attention on the impact of parents on household educational investment. Based on the data of China Family Panel Studies in 2014, This paper examines the effects of parents' cognitive ability on household educational investment for their children. The research propositions were tested using multiple regression analysis methods. Results indicate that parents' cognitive ability can significantly improve the level of monetary and non-monetary investment in education. We also find that compared with their counterparts, the cognitive ability of left-behind children's parents fails to affect their household educational investment, due to the "parent-child separation effect". Further analysis shows that improving the regional informatization level of parents of left-behind children can alleviate the "parent-child separation effect", and finally facilitate cognitive ability's role in increasing household educational investment. These findings enlighten education policy makers and households a feasible way to alleviate the imbalance and insufficiency of household educational investment among left-behind children families.

records.title: Genetic associations with parental investment from conception to wealth inheritance in six cohorts
records.abstract: Genetic inheritance is not the only way parents' genes may affect children. It is also possible that parents' genes are associated with investments into children's development. We examined evidence for links between parental genetics and parental investments, from the prenatal period through to adulthood, using data from six population-based cohorts in the UK, US and New Zealand, together totalling 36,566 parents. Our findings revealed associations between parental genetics-summarized in a genome-wide polygenic score-and parental behaviour across development, from smoking in pregnancy, breastfeeding in infancy, parenting in childhood and adolescence, to leaving a wealth inheritance to adult children. Effect sizes tended to be small at any given time point, ranging from RR = 1.12 (95% confidence interval (95%CI) 1.09, 1.15) to RR = 0.76 (95%CI 0.72, 0.80) during the prenatal period and infancy; β = 0.07 (95%CI 0.04, 0.11) to β = 0.29 (95%CI 0.27, 0.32) in childhood and adolescence, and RR = 1.04 (95%CI 1.01, 1.06) to RR = 1.11 (95%CI 1.07, 1.15) in adulthood. There was evidence for accumulating effects across development, ranging from β = 0.15 (95%CI 0.11, 0.18) to β = 0.23 (95%CI 0.16, 0.29) depending on cohort. Our findings are consistent with the interpretation that parents pass on advantages to offspring not only via direct genetic transmission or purely environmental paths, but also via genetic associations with parental investment from conception to wealth inheritance.

records.title: The Education Policy Agenda and Education Research in Africa : Concerning Mainly Primary Education
records.abstract: This paper reviews the education policy agenda and trends in research relating mainly to primary education in Africa.Sub-Saharan Africa is the region in the world where the spread of primary and secondary education has proliferated the least.Naturally, the situation in Africa differs considerably from country to country, but sub-Saharan countries also share common issues.Almost all the countries in this region face, to varying degrees, problems relating to the legacy of colonialism, political and economic problems, HIV/AIDS at epidemic levels, and conflicts or disputes among ethnic groups, among others.As seen in the World Declaration on Education for All (1990), the Dakar Framework for Action (2000), and the UN Millennium Development Goals, achieving Education for All (EFA), starting with universal primary education, is an urgent and vital issue in the international community.Although the number of children not in school fell by 21 million from 1999 to 2004, there are still 77 million who do not go to school, and the majority of them are concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa.The region has a shortage of the talented, motivated teachers needed to reach EFA goals: in Sub-Saharan Africa the number of teachers will need to increase from 2.4 million in 2004 to 4.0 million in 2015.In recent years, there has been more research carried out in Japan about education in Africa than had previously been the case.Nonetheless, Japanese researchers in this field are still not numerous; many more research papers on this subject are being published by non-Japanese researchers.This paper reviews research trends and discusses a number of important issues relating to the education policy agenda in Africa, such as improving access to primary education; policies relating to grade repetition and promotion; policies for making primary education free; and decentralization, privatization, and community participation.Finally, this paper also touches on problems related to the formation of opinions by aid organizations.

records.title: Compulsory Education Reform, Family Barriers and Female Labour Supply in Turkey: Regression Discontinuity Design with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
records.abstract: Abstract This study investigates heterogeneous treatment effects of compulsory education reform in Turkey on demand for education and labour supply decisions across gender groups and family status using a Regression Discontinuity Design. Although increasing the compulsory schooling years has successfully narrowed the gender gap in labour supply, we find that this effect was only through higher labor force participation of single women and women without children. In other words, our results signify that marriage and fertility have shadowed the human capital effect of higher education. Therefore, policymakers should mainly focus on supply-side policies to mitigate family barriers to raise female labour force participation in Turkey. JEL Classification: J12, J13, J22, J24

records.title: Transforming food systems under climate change through innovation. By BruceCampbell, PhilipThornton, Ana MariaLoboguerrero, DhanushDinesh, AndreeaNowak (Eds.), Cambridge University Press. 2023. pp. 231. ISBN: 9781009227216.
records.abstract: The global food systems' current trajectory falls short of attaining the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by 2030, necessitating an urgent appraisal of the barriers impeding progress. Population growth places a substantial strain on food production and distribution systems, exacerbating the challenges our world faces. Concurrently, poverty and inequality significantly contribute to depriving a substantial portion of the world's population of access to affordable and nutritious food. Climate change further compounds the predicament, affecting agricultural productivity through its impact on weather patterns, soil fertility, and water availability. Extreme weather events, such as droughts and floods, disrupt food production, while unsustainable farming practices contribute to deforestation, land degradation, and biodiversity loss. Transforming Food Systems Under Climate Change through Innovation, a collaborative work authored by esteemed experts and researchers, offers a comprehensive framework for understanding the multifaceted problems and envisioning a sustainable future. This invaluable publication sheds light on the obstacles at hand while presenting practical solutions and actionable insights. By emphasizing the pivotal role of research as a catalyst for transformative change and advocating for collaborative partnerships, the book equips policymakers and advisors with the necessary tools to drive tangible transformations on the ground. The contributors clearly break down a variety of strategies for transforming the food system throughout the 19 chapters in this book. Chapters 1 through 3 introduce what the problem is, why change is needed, and suggest solution strategies. The bulk of the book presents actions dependent on a realignment of the enablers of change in food systems, structures, and society, to ensure that our policies, institutions, and innovations foster and finance transformation: Chapters 4 through 6 tackle financial constraints and climate investment, Chapters 7 through 10 highlight climate vulnerability and farming strategies, and Chapters 11 through 15 continue the topic of finance, recommend policy and organizational changes, and provides alternative innovative theories which add guidance on engagement, partnership, and research transformation. Finally, the book concludes with Chapters 16 through 19 proposing a reimagining of the future. Ultimately, the clear sectioning of the book creates an accessible guide for specific topics and includes a larger variety of expertise. Chapter 1, titled “Fixing Our Broken Food System,” emphasizes the imperative of establishing sustainable and equitable food systems to address the impact on every SDG. The authors argue that despite past achievements, current food systems are failing, highlighting the necessity of transformative actions. This section illuminates the role of individual behavior, policies and institutions, research and innovation, and partnerships and alliances as catalysts for the much-needed transformation. Additionally, the authors advocate for outcome-oriented agricultural research for development (AR4D) to facilitate targeted transformation, maximizing benefits while minimizing trade-offs. In the second chapter, the focus is on complex food systems requiring transformation for global food security and answering climate-related difficulties. It identifies four major interlocking elements for driving change, including redirecting systems and livelihoods, understanding climate impacts, tackling emerging environmental issues, and realigning the “enablers of change.” This portion proposes eleven specific actions to achieve these objectives, detailing goals, mechanisms, geographic areas, and stakeholders. Last, Chapter 3 recognizes research as a catalyst for change within food-system transformation, diagnosing problems, setting targets, developing solutions, and scaling them on the ground. This part of the book affirms research, innovation, and transformative approaches in food system routing, socio-cultural issues, risk reduction, responses to environmental challenges, and enabling factors like policies, regulation, finance, and innovation. The authors of Chapter 4 stresses the critical importance of preserving high-carbon ecosystems, such as forests, peatlands, and mangroves, for climate change mitigation due to their significant carbon storage capacity in limited areas. They articulate how agricultural expansion, which displaces these ecosystems, contributes to climate change, and preventing further land conversion requires collaboration among individuals, indigenous communities, policies, institutions, and investments. In Chapter 5, the authors continue the discussion by asserting that well-designed markets and public-sector actions can promote climate-resilient agriculture and improve livelihood opportunities for farmers. They outline the need for collaboration between the public and private sectors to create advantageous markets for small-scale farmers while reducing risks. Chapter 6 maintains that redirecting farming and rural livelihoods towards new trajectories can address impediments such as youth unemployment and failing food systems. They propose actions to invest in rural industries, enhance financial services and skills, improve automation and tools, provide training and re-skilling opportunities, and implement safety-net programs. These actions must be inclusive of women in farming and disenfranchised rural youth prone to migration. Chapter 7 delves into climate resilience within the climate-security nexus, highlighting the risks embedded in the negative cycle of fragility, climate vulnerability, and human insecurity, while emphasizing the transformative potential of enhancing society's climate resilience. Chapter 8 proposes the use of climate services and agricultural advisory services to assist farmers in managing climate-related risks. Additionally, Chapter 9 insists on shifting to low-emission diets that promote health and sustainability to meet climate targets, particularly through scaling up plant-based meat production. Chapter 10 accentuates the value chain interventions required to solve the significant environmental impact of food loss and waste, emphasizing the need for interventions at various stages to effectively reduce waste. All four segments underscore the need for climate resilience, transformative actions, and interventions throughout the value chain to mitigate risks, enhance sustainability, and promote positive outcomes in areas such as food security, agriculture, and environmental conservation. Additionally, this portion of the book spotlights the importance of collaboration among individuals, communities, policies, institutions, and investments to achieve meaningful change, as well as the interconnected nature of climate-related challenges. Chapter 11 asserts the importance of navigating complex multi-level governance and adapting policies to local contexts in achieving transformative and sustainable outcomes in global food systems under climate change. It advocates for an anticipatory governance approach, inclusive stakeholder processes, and a gendered lens to challenge the status quo and create an enabling policy environment. These principles extend to financial decisions, as discussed in Chapter 12, where cooperation between development finance actors and the private sector is essential for closing funding gaps and mobilizing capital resources. Chapter 13 indicates the need for collective action to include marginalized groups in agricultural development and climate-resilient food security. Chapter 14 accents the dimensions of innovation required for food system transformation, including the design and management of transformative innovations and the engagement of innovation organizations with the wider ecosystem. Finally, Chapter 15 proposes theory of change (ToC) approaches to guide engagement, partnership, and research in the complex domain of AR4D. The concluding passages of the book feature the importance of leadership and partnerships in driving transformative change across different scales and actors within the research systems. The authors accentuate the critical role of research and innovation in food system transformation and stress the need for substantial investments from both public and private sectors, coupled with ongoing feedback and measurement using transdisciplinary approaches. They advocate for the reevaluation and restructuring of current research systems, including the possibility of phasing out, reorienting, or creating new institutions and initiatives. This transformative process requires introspection, effective leadership, and a commitment to overcoming obstacles to fully harness the potential of research and innovation systems in achieving the necessary food system transformation. This book makes a significant contribution to the existing literature on the transformation of food systems. It aligns itself with recently published reports that reiterate the urgent need for radical change in global food systems. By incorporating perspectives from a diverse team of researchers and capturing various fields such as climate, environment, agriculture, and the social sciences, the book imparts valuable insights and expertise, enriching the academic debate on this topic. In addition, the decision to include free access to the book through Open Access on Cambridge Core further enhances its impact and accessibility. The book's methodology is rooted in a global interdisciplinary approach, leveraging the collective knowledge and expertise of a diverse team of researchers and editors. By combining insights from multiple disciplines and drawing upon various tools and approaches, the authors produce a comprehensive analysis and synthesis of the subject matter. The inclusion of different perspectives and the emphasis on inclusivity and diversity strengthen the book's arguments and make it a valuable resource for researchers and students seeking a comprehensive understanding of food system transformation. Ultimately, the book helps readers understand the need for transformative changes in global food systems and presents insights into various aspects of food system transformation. The book aims to provide practical, actionable insights for policymakers, advisors, researchers, and students interested in undertaking the barriers to food system transformation. Because the book covers such a wide range of topics there is not an in-depth analysis of a single topic, however, that is not the intent or scope of this book. In fact, this book offers a starting point for future field-specific research and scholarship. Data sharing is not applicable to this article as no new data were created or analyzed in this study.

records.title: Has the educational progress in China exacerbated the deviation of fertility intention from fertility behavior?
records.abstract: Abstract The discrepancy between fertility intentions and fertility behavior has been a common occurrence, yet there is no consensus regarding the impact of education on fertility deviations and the underlying mechanisms. Drawing on data from the Chinese General Social Survey (CGSS) conducted in 2017, this study examines the influence of education on fertility deviations and investigates the mediating mechanisms through which education affects such deviations. The findings reveal that the relationship between education and fertility deviation is not simply linear.The individuals with both lower and higher levels of education are prone to deviate from their intended fertility, but in contrasting ways. Those with lower level of education tend to exhibit lower fertility intentions compared to their actual fertility behavior, whereas the reverse is observed among individuals with higher education levels. As educational attainment increases, the phenomenon of fertility intentions surpassing actual behavior becomes more pronounced. The stepwise regression analysis of the mediating effect and the results of the KHB decomposition demonstrate that personal income and age of first marriage serve as mediators in the educational influence on fertility deviation, with the latter playing a particularly significant role. Based on these findings, the following recommendations are proposed: shortening the duration of compulsory education and lower the legal age of marriage; redefine the concept of educational involution and decrease the financial burden of children's education; promote balanced development of basic education and bridge the educational disparities between urban and rural areas.

records.title: Educational Investment for Future Marriage? Evidence of Missing Girls from China
records.abstract: Abstract Numerous studies have shown that a sex ratio imbalance (more boys than girls in a society) may result in a sequence of social problems. This study investigated the expected effect of a high sex ratio on educational investment. Using nationally representative data from the China Family Panel Studies and the 2010 Census, we determined the following: (i) a high sex ratio increased educational expenditure for boys relative to girls; (ii) parents who took education seriously and who cared about their children's education were more likely to invest in education to appear attractive in the future marriage market, and (iii) the profound impact of a high sex ratio on educational expenditure was more pronounced in less educated and poorer families. Our findings raised the possibility that the effect of the sex ratio may bring about more gender inequality in the future. The implicit cost of a high sex ratio may further lead to a vicious cycle of family fertility and childbearing.

records.title: The Empirical Study: Psychopathy, Fertility, Longevity, Interacting Phenotypes, and Parental Effects
ANALYZING THE IMPACTS OF POPULATION AGING ON NATIONAL ECONOMIES
records.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
records.abstract: This article analyzes the impacts of population aging on national economies, focusing on key aspects such as the definition of population aging, economic challenges arising from it, impacts on economic sectors, and the need for proactive policies and strategies to mitigate negative effects. Population aging refers to the increase in the proportion of elderly individuals in a population, resulting from declining fertility rates and increased life expectancy. This demographic shift poses significant economic challenges, primarily through decreased labor force participation and increased healthcare and pension costs. The article examines how these challenges affect various economic sectors such as healthcare, labor market dynamics, and government expenditure. It emphasizes the importance of implementing proactive policies and strategies to mitigate these negative effects. These may include measures such as promoting active aging initiatives, encouraging longer working lives, reforms in healthcare systems and retirement schemes, investment in technology and automation, and fostering intergenerational solidarity. By understanding the impacts of population aging on national economies and adopting proactive approaches, policymakers can effectively address the economic consequences of this demographic shift.

records.title: Cliometrics of Growth
Dependence on Forest Products to Sustain Rural Livelihood: An Experience from Bankura Forest, West Bengal
Farmers’ perception towards the changes of land distribution in the Bandarban hill district of Bangladesh
records.abstract: The Chattogram Hill Tracts (CHT) are witnessing an escalating pace of land use change as a result of population dynamics, economic development, climatic change, greater accessibility, and agricultural technical advancements. The study was conducted in Rwanggchhari and Ruma upazila of Bandarban district, Bangladesh. This study explored farmers’ perception towards land use change and the factors contributing to their perception. Following a proportionate random sampling technique, a total of 120 households were sampled and survey was administered through a predesigned close ended questionnaire. A substantial number of respondents (54%) were more than 40 years old, of whom 51% were educated with an average family size was five. The respondents had an average annual income of BDT 91830. An average land holding was 3.59 acres were seen in the study area and these lands were occupied with agricultural, forest, vegetable lands and also with flat and hilly lands. Meanwhile, 98% farmers maintained medium to higher perception towards the changes of land distribution. In addition, out of eight attributes, three attributes, namely, educational attainment, agricultural training received and hill land ownership had significant influence on the perception of land use change by the respondents. The findings of the study can be utilized by the policy makers and planners of the country to formulate future land distribution policy of the CHT in future. Ann. Bangladesh Agric. (2022) 26 (1) : 75-89

records.title: Education Provision and Demographic Change in England and Wales
records.abstract: The provision needed for education has a very direct relationship to annual birth rates and the size of successive age-groups. A contracting industry displays three main features: overmanning, excess plant capacity and rising unit costs. Educational provision must be looked at in broader terms than provision for compulsory schooling between 5 and 16. Unemployment promotes the need for and expectation of the retraining of adults, an extension of further education and training into the adult sector severely limited by constraints upon resources. The ability to produce goods and services to sustain the growing demand for social services lies at the heart of national economic problems in the UK and should influence the provision of post-school education and training. The problems of the schools and of higher education resulting from demographic change come together in the teacher training sector. The education industry has so long been accustomed to growth that it has shown itself ill-prepared for contraction.

records.title: Access to Pensions, Old-Age Support, and Child Investment in China
records.abstract: Abstract This paper studies how access to public pensions affects old-age support and child investment in traditional societies. Guided by predictions from an overlapping generations model, we analyze the influences of a new pension program in rural China, using a difference-in-differences approach. We find that the program crowds out transfers from working-age adults, especially men, to their elderly parents. Interestingly, the impact on child investment significantly differs by child gender. While adult parents increase educational investment in sons, their investment in daughters appears to decrease. Our findings highlight the unintended consequences of public pensions on parental investment.
