records.title: Factors Influencing the Numerical and Reading Abilities of Grade 3 Learners in Selected Elementary Schools
records.venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
records.abstract: This study evaluated the numerical and reading abilities of Grade 3 learners in rural and urban schools in Caramoan South District. Specifically, it aimed to (1) determine the numerical and reading abilities of Grade 3 learners across urban and rural school categories; (2) assess the physical learning environment in terms of school buildings, building condition, building materials, room condition, number of makeshift rooms, usable furniture, and other school facilities; (3) determine the social environment in terms of parental involvement and peer influence; (4) describe the socio-economic status of learners in terms of parents’ educational attainment, family income, and family size; and (5) examine the influence of physical learning environment, social environment, socio-economic status, and school location on learners’ numerical and reading abilities. A two-stage sampling design was used, with stratified random sampling to classify schools as urban or rural and simple random sampling to select Grade 3 learners, ensuring proportional representation. Data were gathered with approval from the Public Schools District Supervisor and school heads of six public elementary schools. Secondary data from Google Forms included CRLA, ALNAT, and NSBI for SY 2024–2025, assessing learners’ reading and numeracy abilities and describing the physical learning environment. A structured research questionnaire was developed to gather data on the socio-economic status and social environment of Grade 3 learners. The instrument obtained a Content Validity Index (CVI) of 0.933, indicating high validity. The reliability of the research instrument was determined using Cronbach's Alpha coefficient, with values of 0.70 and above considered acceptable. The computed Cronbach's alpha values ranged from 0.700 to 0.791 for the parental involvement and peer influence scales in literacy and numeracy. Fifteen learners participated in the pilot test. From a population of 427 Grade 3 learners in 17 schools, Yamane’s Formula determined a sample of 207, but 204 respondents (143 urban and 61 rural) were included in the final analysis. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Linear Mixed Models to account for clustering of learners within schools. Results showed that the physical learning environment had a significant negative effect on numeracy, while parental involvement and school location were significant predictors. This may be explained by studies indicating that school facilities alone are not strong predictors of achievement. Hanushek (2003) found that school inputs such as buildings and resources have weak effects on learning, while Hattie (2009) emphasized that teacher quality and instructional practices have a stronger influence on student performance. This means that even in well-equipped schools, learners may still perform poorly if teaching methods and other learning factors are not effective. In addition, family size showed a negative significant relationship with numeracy. For reading abilities, only the physical learning environment emerged as a significant factor, while other variables were not statistically significant. The study concludes that both school-based and home-based factors influence learners’ outcomes and recommends improving physical learning conditions, strengthening parental involvement, and implementing targeted interventions for low-performing learners in numeracy and reading.

records.title: The Emergence of the Child Quantity-Quality Tradeoff - insights from early modern academics
records.abstract: Abstract Consider the transition out of a stagnant Malthusian system spearheaded by high-human-capital people. Individuals with a stronger preference for offspring quality may be the first to escape the Malthusian regime and adopt modern fertility behaviours (Galor and Moav 2002). To test this hypothesis, we examine the relationship between family size and human capital among academics in Northern Europe in the two centuries before the Industrial Revolution. We measure the human capital of academics using a novel approach based on their publications. We find that scholars with a higher number of publications than the median shifted from having more siblings to having fewer siblings in the first half of the 18th century. Estimating the parameters of an evolutionary growth model by indirect inference, we show how Malthusian constraints initially led the high human capital families to reproduce more, before being endogenously replaced by Beckerian constraints with a tradeoff between child quality and quantity. Our results support an extension of Galor and Moav’s (2002) approach, in which the decline of Malthusian constraints is linked to the accumulation of human capital during the 18th century.

records.title: The Effect of Education on Fertility Rates in Asia: A Socioeconomic Bibliometric Analysis
records.abstract: Much empirical evidence has been reported on the impact of educational attainment on fertility rates. Women’s higher education in the past several decades has emerged as a significant factor that determines fertility patterns and broader socioeconomic outcomes. Educational enrollment and attainment remain close ly related to fertility timing, family size, union formation, partnership choices, labor force participation, and broad family behaviors in nations with highly educated populations. Higher education tends to promote late marriages and delayed childbearing for careers and self-improvement. This leads to smaller families and the delay of childbearing until later years of life. In addition, greater autonomy and financial independence through education enable women to make informed choices regarding reproductive health, family planning, and choice of partner. The article reviews scholarly literature on the impact of education on fertility levels in Asia between 2000 and 2024 using bibliometric analysis. The research uses 578 papers drawn from the Web of Science Core Collection to analyze thematic evolution, co-authorship patterns, and the intellectual structure of this interdisciplinary field. Through VOSviewer, the analysis provides three main visualizations: keyword co occurrence networks to identify broad research questions, co-authorship by country to identify international collaboration, and bibliographic coupling to illustrate the intersectionality of intellectual communities at a national level. This broader analysis shows how the debate has evolved over time in response to shifts in population trends, education policy, labor market participation, household decision-making, and socioeco nomic development within Asian countries.

records.title: Assessment of the Socioeconomic Impact of Fuel Subsidy Removal on Transportation in Ile-Ife, Osun State, Nigeria
records.venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Applied Science
records.abstract: Fuel subsidies in Nigeria were originally designed to safeguard energy affordability; their removal has consistently generated fiscal relief at the expense of significant socioeconomic disruption. This study examines the impact of subsidy removal on transportation and household welfare in Ile-Ife, Nigeria. Utilizing a descriptive survey research design, primary data were collected from 370 respondents—including civil servants, traders, and commercial drivers—selected through a multistage sampling technique. The study employed descriptive statistics and a multiple regression model to analyze the relationships between transportation costs (TC), socioeconomic characteristics, and socioeconomic welfare (SW). Findings reveal that average daily transportation fares in Ile-Ife surged by 160% (from ₦250 to ₦650) following the policy change, while daily travel frequency contracted by 33.3% (from 4.2 to 2.8 trips), signaling constrained mobility. Regression analysis confirmed that transportation costs have a significant negative effect on welfare (𝛽 = -0.642, t = -7.55). Furthermore, family size (𝛽 = -0.210) and the number of dependents (𝛽 = -0.305) were identified as significant predictors of increased vulnerability. Conversely, higher monthly income and educational attainment positively influenced coping capacity. Consequently, all three null hypotheses were rejected. The study concludes that fuel subsidy removal disproportionately burdens low-income urban residents through inflationary transport costs and reduced disposable income, highlighting the urgent need for targeted social safety nets and transport policy interventions.

records.title: Young Mothers’ Fertility Decisions and Ideal Family Size in Peri-Urban Indonesia
records.abstract: This study addresses the growing demographic transition in peri-urban Indonesia, where changing socio-economic conditions increasingly shape fertility behaviour yet remain underexplored from women’s subjective perspectives. It examines how young mothers construct their perceptions of ideal family size and make fertility decisions in Depok Subdistrict, Sleman Regency, Special Region of Yogyakarta. Using a descriptive qualitative approach, the research involved married women aged 20–35 years with one or two children. Data were collected through in-depth interviews in Condongcatur and Maguwoharjo villages and analysed thematically.Findings indicate that most respondents perceive two children as the ideal family size, driven primarily by economic considerations, aspirations for quality childcare, and the need to balance reproductive and productive roles. Contextual variations arise from gender composition preferences and emotional motivations such as sibling companionship. Fertility decisions are influenced by household economic conditions, educational attainment, employment status, and the perceived function of family planning as a birth-spacing mechanism rather than a family-size determinant. Social pressure from extended families remains limited.This study contributes novel qualitative evidence on fertility norm internalisation in peri-urban contexts, highlighting how economic rationality increasingly replaces traditional pronatalist influences in shaping reproductive choices. It offers policy-relevant insights for context-sensitive family planning interventions.

records.title: Fertility rates and their impact on nations: a comparison between India and other countries
records.abstract: This editorial is written in response to the article “Responding to declining global fertility rates” published in the January 10, 2026, issue of The Lancet.[1] The article highlighted the challenges posed by declining birth rates and their impact on national growth and social structures. It also presented some striking measures adopted by various countries to boost fertility rates. One particularly noteworthy example was China’s decision to increase taxes on condom sales, presumably to encourage higher rates of unintended pregnancies. Given that we grew up in India, the world’s most populous country, with approximately 1.46 billion people, the global trend of declining fertility rates is quite surprising. In contrast, India has long been concerned with rapid population growth and the challenges of ensuring adequate food, shelter, and employment for its large population. WHAT IS THE FERTILITY RATE? The total fertility rate (TFR) of a country or community refers to the average number of children a woman is expected to have over her lifetime. It is a key indicator used to estimate the population’s replacement level in a given nation or geographic region. Historically, the global TFR ranged from 5 to 7.5 births per woman around 1800, but declined to approximately 2.3 in 2023. According to United Nations projections, this figure is expected to decrease further to about 1.8 by 2100, below replacement level. The replacement level is generally considered to be 2.1 births per woman, sufficient to maintain a stable population. However, in countries with higher infant, child, or adult mortality rates, the replacement level may be higher. To better understand these trends, it is important to adopt a holistic perspective on fertility rates across different countries and examine how rising or declining population levels influence their social and economic structures. As it is not feasible to discuss each country individually in this editorial, selected countries have been grouped for comparative analysis. EAST ASIA: CHINA, SOUTH KOREA, AND JAPAN China’s TFR is approximately 1.55, well below the replacement level. The country’s one-child policy, enforced from 1980 to 2016, significantly altered its demographic structure and contributed to sustained fertility decline. In response, the government revised its policy in 2016 to allow two children per couple, and further expanded it in 2021 to permit up to three children. South Korea currently has one of the lowest fertility rates in the world, reaching critically low levels. In 2022, the TFR was reported at just 0.78, far below replacement level, with the capital city, Seoul, recording an even lower rate of 0.57. Japan reported a TFR of 1.26 in 2022 and is facing the dual challenge of a rapidly aging population and persistently low birth rates. The country’s population declined by approximately 430,000 in 2018. Limited immigration has further compounded the issue, contributing to a shrinking labor force.[2-5] INDIA AND NEIGHBORING COUNTRIES India is currently the most populous country in the world. Its TFR has declined markedly over the decades, from 5.2 in 1971 to 2.2 in 2018, and further to 2.1 in 2020, reaching the replacement level. While food security has improved and housing development is being prioritized, generating sufficient employment opportunities for the growing youth population remains a significant challenge. Bangladesh has also achieved notable success in fertility reduction through widespread access to contraception across all sections of society. Its TFR declined from 6.8 in 1975 to 2.0 in 2020, a considerable accomplishment given its high population density. Pakistan, with a TFR of 3.2, remains above the replacement level. As a developing country with limited resources, its rapidly expanding population raises concerns about the ability to provide adequate food, housing, and employment. This growth has been attributed to limited access to family planning, as well as sociocultural, religious, and political influences. However, this relationship is complex, as several Muslim-majority countries such as Iran, Türkiye, Qatar, and the Maldives have achieved TFRs below 2. Nepal and Sri Lanka have maintained fertility rates close to the replacement level. Afghanistan, on the other hand, has a relatively high TFR of 4.4. However, in the context of ongoing conflict, higher mortality rates, and limited healthcare infrastructure, this rate may be interpreted differently.[3-5] EUROPEAN NATIONS Fertility rates across Europe remain low, with no country currently achieving a TFR above 2.0. France, with a TFR of 1.9, has the highest rate in the region. In contrast, Italy reports a much lower TFR of 1.26, largely attributed to financial constraints faced by couples and the burden of supporting an aging population. Norway also has a relatively low TFR of 1.57, with delayed marriages contributing to reduced population growth. Other European countries similarly report sub-replacement fertility levels: Denmark (1.72), Portugal (1.35), Spain (1.19), and Greece (1.43). The United Kingdom has a TFR of 1.53 despite substantial inflows of migrants. Ukraine and Russia report TFRs of 1.57 and 1.6, respectively. Ongoing conflict between the two nations since 2022, along with significant war-related casualties, is likely to have further contributed to population decline.[3-5] AFRICAN NATIONS Most African countries continue to exhibit high total TFRs. Niger has the highest reported TFR at 6.64, followed by Angola (5.7) and the Democratic Republic of Congo (5.49). In Nigeria, although fertility remains high, it has declined from 6.35 in 1960 to 5.3 in 2019. Elevated fertility rates in Sub-Saharan Africa are often associated with factors such as early marriage, limited use of contraception, and the strong social value placed on childbearing. In contrast, North African countries demonstrate comparatively lower TFRs, with Tunisia at 1.93, Egypt at 2.41, Morocco at 2.25, and Algeria at 2.7.[3-5] USA, CANADA, AND LATIN AMERICA The TFR in the United States is currently below the replacement level of 2.1, though it remains comparatively higher than in many other developed countries. Fertility rates are generally lower among the native-born population and higher among immigrant groups, which helps support overall population growth. In Canada, TFR is well below the replacement level, with recent estimates around 1.25 children per woman, reflecting a sustained long-term decline. To address demographic imbalances and support economic growth, the government actively encourages immigration, particularly among skilled workers. Across Latin America, fertility rates have declined sharply in recent decades and are now generally at or below replacement level. The regional average TFR is about 1.8 children per woman, with most countries below the replacement threshold of 2.1. Country-specific estimates include Brazil (around 1.7–1.8), Mexico (about 1.7), Colombia (around 1.9), Argentina (approximately 1.5–2.1), Peru (around 2.0), and Venezuela (around 2.0–2.2). This decline reflects broader social and economic changes, including improved education, greater participation of women in the workforce, and wider access to contraception.[3-5] REASONS FOR LOW FERTILITY Socio-economic difficulties. Postponement of marriage and childbearing. Dual-income households (both partners working). Economic pressures, including rising housing costs and limited employment opportunities. Global instability and pessimism about the future. REASONS FOR HIGH FERTILITY ✓ Early marriage. ✓ Limited access to contraception. ✓ Religious influences. ✓ Prevailing social norms and cultural beliefs. ✓ High rates of infant and child mortality. ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES OF LOW FERTILITY ❖ A smaller proportion of young, non-disabled individuals can lead to labor shortages in key sectors such as industry, agriculture, and defense, resulting in imbalances between labor demand and supply. ❖ Rising life expectancy has increased the proportion of older adults. This demographic shift is a concern, as older populations generally require more healthcare support and may contribute less to economic productivity. ❖ A decline in the working-age population may reduce tax revenues, while spending on pensions and elderly care is likely to increase, placing added pressure on public finances. ❖ On the positive side, low fertility is often linked to higher per capita income, as seen in many countries with low TFRs. In contrast, regions with higher TFRs tend to have lower per capita income. ❖ Another advantage is that natural resources are distributed among a smaller population, thereby reducing pressure on them. Reducing fossil fuel consumption may also help slow global warming. MEASURES ADOPTED BY COUNTRIES TO PROMOTE FERTILITY AND INCREASE BIRTH RATES ➣ Some countries have imposed taxes on contraceptives such as condoms,[1,5] while simultaneously offering financial incentives to encourage childbearing. For example, couples may receive benefits of around USD 500 per child under age 3. ➣ In South Korea, the government has introduced initiatives such as state-supported dating services, exemptions from compulsory military service, subsidized housing, and childcare facilities. Despite multiple efforts over the past decade, these measures have had limited success. ➣ Japan has increased budgetary allocations to boost fertility, including financial incentives, free education for children, paternity leave, and more flexible maternity leave policies. ➣ In Hungary, policies include lifelong income tax exemptions for mothers with two or more children to incentivize higher birth rates. ➣ Romania, during the period 1967–1989, implemented strict pronatalist policies such as banning contraception and abortion, along with imposing taxes on childless couples. However, these measures led to serious adverse consequences, including the deaths of approximately 9000 women due to unsafe illegal abortions.[4] PROBLEMS ASSOCIATED WITH HIGH FERTILITY Countries with high fertility rates often face multiple socioeconomic challenges. These include low per capita income, poor nutrition, high child mortality, and limited access to education, which in turn lead to low-paying employment opportunities. In such settings, household income must be shared among many children, resulting in reduced living standards for the entire family. Cultural and religious beliefs can also help maintain a high TFR. MEASURES ADOPTED TO CONTROL FERTILITY AND REDUCE BIRTH RATES Various governments have attempted to reduce population growth through coercive measures, including forced sterilization.[4] In India, during the Emergency, large-scale sterilization campaigns were implemented nationwide. These policies led to significant public backlash, contributing to the government’s electoral defeat, and sterilization rates declined sharply thereafter. Similar coercive measures were attempted in parts of Europe and North America in the early twentieth century, but proved ineffective. More recently, in Peru in the 1990s, forced sterilization programs targeting indigenous populations also failed and raised serious ethical concerns. According to international standards, including those of the United Nations, decisions regarding the number and spacing of children should rest entirely with individuals or couples, emphasizing the importance of reproductive rights and informed choice. CONCLUSION Countries with low TFRs are working to raise birth rates, largely due to concerns about aging populations and a shrinking workforce. However, advances in artificial intelligence, automation, and robotics may help sustain productivity despite a smaller labor force. These technologies could also enable older individuals to remain economically active longer, with retirement policies that are more flexible and tailored to job requirements. In defense, increasing reliance on technologies such as drones and missiles may reduce the need for large standing armies. One potential strategy for low-fertility countries is to encourage immigration of skilled and productive individuals from regions with higher fertility and limited job opportunities. At the same time, host countries must carefully address challenges related to demographic balance and social integration. A large youth population in developing countries is not inherently beneficial unless supported by adequate employment opportunities and effective skills development. Without these, rising unemployment may contribute to social instability and law-and-order issues. Countries with high population growth should avoid coercive measures, such as forced sterilization, which have proven ineffective in the past. Instead, emphasis should be placed on raising awareness through community leaders and educators, highlighting the benefits of smaller families, including improved living standards, better education, and enhanced overall well-being for future generations. Financial support and sponsorship Nil. Conflicts of interest There are no conflicts of interest.

records.title: Advancing the Curriculum in Response to Job Market Needs
records.abstract: Higher education faces increasing imperatives to align curricula with evolving workforce demands driven by technological advancement, automation, and demographic transitions. This article examines Georgia Southern University's strategic response through a partnership between its Institute for Innovative and Integrative Studies (now University College) and the University Libraries to develop an Information Studies concentration within the Bachelor of Interdisciplinary Studies program. Library faculty successfully developed and implemented six new courses offering stackable, competency-based instruction in metaliteracy, data literacy, artificial intelligence, intellectual property, digital humanities, and special topics competencies valued in contemporary labor markets. Through systematic curriculum design, targeted professional development, and programmatic assessment frameworks, library faculty transitioned from traditional instructional support roles to delivering credit-bearing courses that integrate transdisciplinary competencies fundamental to workforce preparedness. This initiative demonstrates that academic libraries can evolve into substantive pedagogical partners, providing flexible educational pathways that enhance student readiness while addressing enrollment challenges through accessible interdisciplinary programming.

records.title: Human capital differences and fertility inequality: an analysis based on the substitutability and complementarity of educational investment factors
records.abstract: Abstract China’s persistently low fertility is associated with fertility inequality, reflected in a U-shaped relationship between household human capital and fertility. We develop an overlapping-generations model showing that this pattern depends on the substitutability of educational inputs. When educational inputs are complementary, fertility is U-shaped in household human capital, with middle-human-capital households having the fewest children; when inputs are substitutable, the relationship is inverted U-shaped. Using China Family Panel Studies data, we find a robust U-shaped relationship between household human capital and fertility, significant complementarity among educational time, monetary investment, and household human capital in children’s human-capital formation, and similar patterns across eastern, central, and western China. Complementarity requires households to increase time and monetary inputs jointly, intensifying the quantity–quality trade-off, particularly for middle-human-capital households. Policies that enhance substitutability among educational inputs may therefore mitigate fertility inequality and raise aggregate fertility.

records.title: The relationship between economic status, poverty, and health among Arabs in Israel
records.venue: Israel Journal of Health Policy Research
records.abstract: Abstract Background Arabs in Israel, comprising about 21% of the population, are recognized as an indigenous minority with full citizenship rights, yet they face persistent structural disadvantages compared to Jewish citizens. These disparities are evident across socioeconomic, educational, employment, and health domains. High poverty rates, particularly among women, children, and the older adults, are aggravated by limited governmental investment in infrastructure, education, and health services. Arab women’s labor force participation remains notably low due to systemic barriers. Extensive evidence links socioeconomic status with health outcomes and behaviors. This study examines how sociodemographic factors and health knowledge are associated with economic status, self-rated health, and health behaviors among Arabs in Israel. Methods This cross-sectional study utilized data from the 2015–2016 Health and Environment Survey among Arabs in Israel (HESPI). Employing a three-stage stratified cluster sampling of over 2,000 households, face-to-face interviews gathered socio-demographic, economic, and health-related data. The final sample included 2,041 adults representing diverse socioeconomic and geographic groups within Arab communities. Results Approximately half of participants lived below the poverty line (51.7%). Those with lower economic status exhibited poorer self-rated health ( p <.001, d = 0.22), higher prevalence of chronic illness ( p =.009, d = 0.13), and lower engagement in physical activity ( p <.001, d = 0.29), while smoking and BMI did not significantly differ by economic status. Family size moderated the relationships between economic status and both chronic illness ( p <.001, 95%CI = 1.33, 2.19) and SRH ( p <.001, 95%CI = -0.33, -0.13), indicating that smaller families are less likely to experience these negative effects of low economic status. Educational attainment slightly moderated the link between economic status and physical activity ( p =.016, η2 = 0.003). Regression analyses revealed that gender, age, education, and health knowledge were significantly associated with health outcomes and behaviors (R 2 = 0.10 to R 2 = 0.43), with health knowledge mediating several of these associations. Conclusions The findings indicate that poverty is associated with poorer health outcomes and behaviors among Arabs in Israel. Smaller family size and higher education may mitigate the negative effects of poverty, and health knowledge plays a mediating role for health outcomes and behaviors. Findings suggest that socioeconomic empowerment and higher education are important in promoting health equity.

records.title: IncuVision: Android-Based Egg Incubator with Machine Learning Algorithm using OpenCV
records.venue: PUP Journal of Science and Technology
records.abstract: The poultry industry is a key part of the Philippines' agricultural sector, with chicken eggs playing a vital role. Traditional methods of assessing egg fertility, such as manual candling, are time-consuming and prone to human error. Despite advancements, local poultry farms still rely on manual methods, lacking automated and real-time monitoring systems, resulting in unreliable evaluations. This study developed IncuVision, an Android-based egg incubator application that uses machine learning and OpenCV to enhance egg monitoring and fertility detection. The app provides real-time data on egg status, monitors embryo development stages, and generates data visualizations. The system was evaluated through feedback from IT faculty, an advisory committee, and egg farmers, focusing on functional suitability, performance efficiency, reliability, and usability. The system achieved a General Weighted Mean (GWM) of 4.30, highlighting its success in delivering an efficient, user-friendly, and reliable tool for egg incubation monitoring. These findings demonstrate the app’s potential to modernize hatchery operations through automated monitoring and real-time notifications. SDG 9 – Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure by introducing intelligent digital solutions that modernize agricultural practices, promote the use of innovative technologies, and strengthen infrastructure in the poultry sector through automation and real-time data systems. The integration of AI and mobile technology can help optimize incubation processes and foster more sustainable and technologically advanced poultry farming practices.

records.title: When Trade Raises Fertility: The Role of Women's Labor Market Attachment
Effect of Aging Population on Labour Productivity in Japan
records.abstract: Japan is one of the clearest developed-economy cases for examining how population aging affects labour productivity. The country combines a very high share of older persons, a shrinking working-age population, long life expectancy, low fertility, and persistent labour shortages. This paper examines the effect of aging population on labour productivity in Japan using a literature-based and secondary-data approach. It draws mainly on recent evidence from the OECD, International Monetary Fund, World Bank, Statistics Bureau of Japan, Cabinet Office of Japan, and peer-reviewed studies published from 2020 onward. The analysis shows that aging affects labour productivity through four main channels: reduction in labour supply, change in the age composition of workers, pressure on firms to reorganize work, and the need for stronger technology adoption. Aging may reduce productivity where firms rely on labour-intensive routines, weak training systems, mandatory retirement, or low labour mobility. However, the effect is not automatically negative. Older workers can support productivity when their experience is retained, when tasks are redesigned, and when firms invest in ICT, automation, artificial intelligence, and continuous training. The paper concludes that Japan's productivity challenge is not simply that the population is older; it is that many labour-market and firm-level systems have not adjusted fast enough to an older workforce. Policy should therefore focus on lifelong learning, flexible retirement, stronger ICT use, improved labour mobility, productivity upgrading in small and medium-sized enterprises, and better inclusion of women, older workers, and skilled foreign workers. Keywords: Aging population; labour productivity; Japan; older workers; ICT; automation; labour shortages.

records.title: Assessing the effects of child-care subsidies on fertility and birth outcomes: evidence from the child and dependent care tax credit
records.venue: Review of Economics of the Household
records.abstract: Abstract We examine the impact of the Child and Dependent Care Tax Credit (CDCTC) on fertility and birth outcomes. The CDCTC subsidizes child care for working families, thus potentially incentivizing families to have more children or increase investment in child quality. Using the Panel Study of Income Dynamics and the National Center for Health Statistics’ Natality data, we analyze the effects of state-level CDCTC policies on fertility and birth outcomes. We find that the CDCTC has no effects on the probability of having a birth or on birth outcomes; however, the CDCTC does increase labor force participation rates for married mothers.

records.title: L26/P-575 Digital Desire: the rise of Artificial Intelligence relationships and techno-intimacy; impact on future fertility, reproduction, family building and mental health
records.abstract: Abstract Study question What are the motivations for Artificial Intelligence (AI) relationships and potential impact on fertility, future reproduction, family building and mental health Summary answer While some report positive mental health, AI relationships appear to contribute to delayed partnership formation, reduced sexual activity and declining intentions toward family building. What is known already The last two decades saw an increase in dating platforms as individuals tuned to digital platforms for relationships and to fulfil family-building intentions.Recently, advances in AI have extended beyond productivity and automation into the deeply personal domain of human relationships. Increasingly, individuals are turning to AI-powered chatbots and virtual-companions for emotional support, companionship, and, romantic/intimate connections as the lines between psychological-support and relationships blur.This trend is increasing, particularly among younger generations already navigating economic uncertainty and changing social-norms.While these technologies may offer comfort and accessibility, growing reliance may have significant implications for reproductive decision-making as global fertility-rates continue to drop. Study design, size, duration This research aimed to synthesise current evidence on the emerging trend of AI relationships. This systematic literature review was conducted following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic-Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Databases searched included Embase, MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for studies investigating human and AI romantic or intimate relationships. Participants/materials, setting, methods Due to the novelty of the topic as a rapidly emerging use of technology, with limited but gradually increasing peer-reviewed published work, grey literature and pre-print articles were included. Only studies published in English were included. Studies identified were from 2022-2026. Content was analysed and categorised thematically. Main results and the role of chance After screening and full-text assessment, 32 studies were included; USA (12), UK (2), Norway (2) were the top countries but majority of studies reported data from global online analysis with high numbers from Asia. Most participants were in their twenties and thirties, peak reproductive-age. Methods included surveys and interviews ranging from 8 to 1131 for specific user samples; and qualitative content analysis of user-generated content of international app users from mixed online platforms like Replika, and Character.AI. including up to 30,000 conversations. Motivation and positive impact include greater emotional comfort, increased feelings of support, stress relief and support for socially anxious users. Negative consequences included overdependence, emotional addiction; isolation and social withdrawal; stigma and shame; data privacy and manipulation fears and emotional distress when AI identity changes or fails. Mental health effects associated with intensive AI companionship were mixed, suggesting both potential emotional support and increased loneliness depending on user vulnerability and usage patterns. Studies also report altered intimacy patterns, reduced motivation for human romantic relationships, and changes in sexual behaviour. In terms of impact on future reproduction, these factors may plausibly influence reproductive-timing, likelihood of conception, delayed partner-formation and reduced partnered sexual activity, and engagement with reproductive healthcare. Limitations, reasons for caution Only studies published in English were eligible for inclusion, limiting the generalisability of study findings. As this is a novel research area involving emerging technologies, longitudinal studies are needed to confirm implications on future reproduction, especially at population level. Wider implications of the findings As the trend to substitute AI for human partners continues to rise, these behavioural shifts can have direct implications for fertility-rates and family formation at a population level.Stakeholders including psychologists, reproductive health organisations, HCPs, and policy makers, should consider artificial relationships within the wider contexts of fertility trends and reproductive-wellbeing. Trial registration number No

records.title: Determinants Of Financial Inclusion Among Farmers: Evidence From Lunglei District, Mizoram, India
records.venue: IOSR Journal of Economics and Finance
records.abstract: Financial inclusion is a critical driver of economic development, particularly in rural areas where access to formal financial services remains limited. This study examines the determinants of financial inclusion among farmers in Lunglei district, Mizoram, India, using primary data from 320 farmers. A comprehensive set of nonparametric techniques is applied, including Chi-square tests, Spearman rank correlations, Mann–Whitney U tests, and Kruskal–Wallis H tests, to analyse the influence of nine key variables: availability of banks, educational level, distance to the nearest bank, participation in self-help groups (SHGs), financial literacy, household income, age, family size, and reliance on informal moneylenders. The results reveal significant associations between financial inclusion and several factors. Educational level shows the strongest positive association (ρ = 0.417, p < 0.001), explaining approximately 17.39% of the variance in financial inclusion, while distance to the nearest bank exhibits a moderate negative association (ρ = −0.443, p < 0.001). Participation in SHGs (ρ = 0.234, p < 0.001) and household income (ρ = 0.411, p < 0.001) also show positive effects. By contrast, financial literacy and family size are not significantly associated with inclusion levels, challenging conventional assumptions. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of educational attainment, physical access to banking, income enhancement, and community-based institutions in promoting financial inclusion in remote rural settings such as Lunglei district.

The study examines the level of the Multidimensional Poverty (MPI) of minority people of the Diyara region in Malda district, West Bengal, aiming to find out the key variables determining the MPI. The Alkire-Foster methodology has been considered as the base of methodological analysis in the present research. The study found that minority people experience constant socio-economic distress and pronounced deprivation. The study identifies nutrition, education, and employment as pivotal MPI indicators where the community lags, contributing to an exacerbation of MPI scores. The MPI value of the minority of the region is 0.192, which is quite higher than the aggregate value of the district level (0.163), state level (0.097), and even higher than the national level (0.118). Multiple regressions explored that education, age and occupation of the family head; worker ratio of the households and family size are the crucial determining factors of the MPI of minority community in the study area. The study suggests that to alleviate multidimensional poverty, policies aimed at bolstering educational attainment, enhancing public distribution systems, and improving healthcare services are crucial. Additionally, the study highlights the need for unrestricted public infrastructures, like schools and PHCs, and the support of cottage industries to promote sustainable employment. Access to cooking fuel, substandard sanitation, and housing conditions are also identified as critical issues that require immediate attention to improve the lives of the marginalized community in the district of Malda.

records.title: Effectiveness of Reading Remediation Program for Grade One Low Emerging Readers
records.venue: International Journal of Sustainability and Advanced Integrated Research
records.abstract: This study determined the effectiveness of the Reading Remediation Program for Grade One low emerging readers at Baras Pinugay Elementary School, Baras Sub-Office, Division of Rizal, during the School Year 2025–2026. Specifically, it assessed learners' reading performance before and after the intervention in terms of phonics, word recognition, and comprehension and examined differences when grouped according to selected demographic variables. Using an experimental research design, the study involved 32 Grade One low emerging readers who underwent pretest and posttest assessments. Findings revealed that the Reading Remediation Program significantly improved learners' phonics skills and overall reading performance, resulting in higher posttest scores and more learners attaining the Outstanding level. However, improvements in word recognition and comprehension were not statistically significant, indicating that higher-order reading skills require more sustained and targeted instructional support. Most demographic variables, including sex, birth order, family size, parental occupation, mother's educational attainment, and family income, showed no significant influence on posttest reading performance, whereas father's educational attainment significantly affected learners' reading achievement. The study concludes that the Reading Remediation Program is effective in strengthening foundational decoding skills but requires longer implementation and enhanced instructional strategies to improve word recognition and reading comprehension. It is recommended that schools strengthen reading interventions through adequate instructional resources, teacher professional development, targeted comprehension activities, and active parental involvement to further enhance learners' reading outcomes.

records.title: Effects of Comprehension Challenges on the Mathematical Performance of Grade Six Pupils
records.venue: International Journal of Sustainability and Advanced Integrated Research
records.abstract: This study determined the effects of comprehension challenges on the mathematical performance of Grade Six pupils in public elementary schools in District I-C, City Schools Division Office of Antipolo during the School Year 2025–2026. Employing a descriptive survey research design and documentary analysis, the study involved 314 Grade Six pupils selected through simple random sampling from a population of 1,440 using Slovin’s formula. A researcher-made questionnaire was utilized to assess the extent of comprehension challenges affecting mathematical performance in the domains of Number and Number Sense, Measurement and Geometry, Patterns and Algebra, and Statistics and Probability, while pupils’ Mathematics grades were obtained through documentary analysis to determine their level of achievement. Findings revealed that most respondents were female, first-born, belonged to one-child families, came from households with monthly incomes below ₱10,000, had fathers who were college graduates and employed in various occupations, and mothers who were high school graduates and primarily homemakers. Comprehension challenges were found to have a high effect on pupils’ performance in Patterns and Algebra, Measurement and Geometry, and Number and Number Sense, while only a moderate effect was observed in Statistics and Probability. No significant differences were found in the perceived effects of comprehension challenges when respondents were grouped according to sex, sibling position, family size, parents’ educational attainment, parents’ occupation, and monthly family income. Pupils obtained a very satisfactory level of Mathematics achievement, and no significant relationship was established between the perceived effects of comprehension challenges and their Mathematics achievement. The study concluded that demographic characteristics did not significantly influence pupils’ perceptions of comprehension challenges, and that these perceived challenges were not significantly associated with their Mathematics achievement. It is recommended that school administrators strengthen professional development initiatives focusing on mathematics comprehension strategies, teachers integrate explicit mathematical language and reading comprehension instruction into Mathematics lessons, utilize diagnostic assessments to identify comprehension-related learning needs, implement the proposed action plan, and encourage future studies incorporating additional variables

records.title: Parental Involvement Practices in Relation to Kindergarten’s Academic Performance
records.abstract: This study examines the extent of parental involvement practices and their relationship to kindergarten academic performance at Soriano Elementary School during the 2018–2019 school year. Grounded in Epstein’s six-domain framework—parenting, communicating, volunteering, learning at home, decision-making, and collaborating with the community—the study investigates how these dimensions of involvement influence young learners’ outcomes. The objective of the research is threefold: first, to profile parents based on age, marital status, employment, educational attainment, family size, and distance from school; second, to assess the level of involvement across Epstein’s six domains and examine differences across demographic groups; and third, to determine the level of kindergarten academic performance using the Early Childhood Care and Development (ECCD) Checklist, as well as to explore whether parental involvement significantly differs by demographic variables and relates to student performance. A descriptive research design was employed, involving 47 kindergarten parents who completed a validated questionnaire adapted from Epstein’s framework. Responses were analyzed using frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation, z-tests, and Pearson’s r correlation. Results showed that parents’ demographic profiles skewed toward younger, unmarried, employed individuals with undergraduate education, small families, and proximity to school. Overall parental involvement was moderate (mean ≈ 3.29), with parenting and learning at home showing higher engagement, while volunteering and community collaboration were lower. The kindergarteners’ academic performance averaged 106.38, indicating “average overall development.” Significant differences in parental involvement were found only for highest educational attainment, with college graduates showing notably higher involvement (z-tests, p < 0.05). Most other demographic groupings (age, marital status, employment, family size, distance) showed no significant differences. Crucially, there was a significant positive relationship between overall parental involvement and kindergarten academic performance (r = 0.235, p = 0.026). In conclusion, the study highlights that while parental involvement is generally moderate, its positive correlation with kindergarten performance underscores the importance of engaging parents—especially through home-based domains like parenting and learning at home. Enhancing parental engagement strategies, particularly among families with lower educational attainment, can potentially boost early academic outcomes.

records.title: How demography shapes the macroeconomic returns to automation
records.abstract: This paper investigates how demographic change interacts with automation to shape long-term macroeconomic outcomes. Using a calibrated general equilibrium model with heterogeneous labor and capital, we simulate five OECD countries with diverse demographic and technological profiles: Republic of Korea, Australia, Italy, Hungary, and Türkiye. Our model replicates key findings from the literature, including the positive relationship between aging and robot accumulation, as well as the growing capital income share at the expense of the labor income share. Beyond these, we uncover several novel insights. First, robot accumulation is driven more by the share of high-skilled labor and production technology than by declining interest rates. Second, while aging initially boosts robotization, this growth is ultimately constrained by the shrinking pool of high-income contributors. Third, only countries with low initial consumption and production relying on low-skilled labor avoid declines in per capita income. Fourth, robotization often replaces rather than expands capital. Fifth, wage convergence between high- and low-skilled workers emerges as a consequence of automation. Finally, increasing general educational attainment does not necessarily raise per capita GDP growth in aging societies undergoing automation. These findings highlight the importance of labor market structure and technological composition in mediating the macroeconomic effects of automation during demographic transitions.

records.title: MICRO-IRRIGATION AND FERTIGATION: A SCIENTIFICALLY DRIVEN APPROACH TO SUSTAINABLE HORTICULTURE
records.abstract: Micro-irrigation and fertigation have emerged as scientifically advanced and resource-efficient approaches for sustainable horticultural production. With increasing pressure on water resources, soil fertility, and agricultural productivity, these technologies provide precise delivery of water and nutrients directly to the plant root zone, thereby enhancing crop growth, yield, and quality while minimizing wastage. Micro-irrigation systems such as drip and sprinkler irrigation improve water-use efficiency, reduce evaporation losses, and support cultivation under water-scarce conditions. Fertigation, the integrated application of fertilizers through irrigation systems, ensures balanced nutrient supply, improves nutrient-use efficiency, and reduces environmental pollution caused by excessive fertilizer application. This approach also supports sustainable soil health management and minimizes nutrient leaching. The integration of automation, sensors, and precision agriculture technologies further strengthens the effectiveness of micro-irrigation and fertigation in modern horticulture. Despite challenges related to installation cost, technical knowledge, and maintenance, these systems are increasingly recognized as essential tools for climate-resilient and environmentally sustainable agriculture. The study highlights the scientific principles, benefits, applications, and future prospects of micro-irrigation and fertigation as innovative strategies for achieving sustainable horticultural development.

records.title: Relationship Amongst Education Family Size and Socio Economic Conditions of Rural Household of Tinsukia, Assam
records.venue: Technix International Journal for Engineering Research
records.abstract: Education, family size, and socio-economic conditions are closely interconnected dimensions that shape the development and well-being of rural households. Understanding their relationship is essential for designing effective educational and rural development policies. The present study examines the relationship among educational attainment, family size, and socio-economic conditions of rural households in Tinsukia district, Assam. A descriptive and analytical research design was adopted, and primary data were collected from selected rural households using a structured interview schedule. Educational attainment of household members, family size, and socio-economic indicators such as income, occupation, parental education, housing conditions, and asset ownership were considered for analysis. The findings are expected to provide empirical evidence on how demographic and socio-economic factors affect educational outcomes in rural Assam. The study offers valuable insights for policymakers, educational planners, and rural development agencies in designing targeted interventions aimed at improving educational opportunities and enhancing the socio-economic well-being of rural communities.

records.title: Peer Review Report For: Knowledge and Attitudes Toward Healthcare Services Among a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG) in Coastal Karnataka, India: Findings from a Community-Based Cross-Sectional Survey [version 2; peer review: 1 approved, 2 approved with reservations]
records.abstract: Background Among various Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) in India, the Koraga community stands out as one that warrants focused attention through targeted public health efforts. Objective A community-based cross-sectional study was conducted to assess knowledge and attitudes toward healthcare services among 622 adult members (aged 18–70 years) of the Koraga tribe from a southern coastal district of Karnataka. Methods We employed a multistage cluster sampling approach, treating each block under the study as a cluster and selecting households using probability proportional to size (PPS) method. Data collection survey occurred from April 2021 to April 2022 through personal interviews with consenting adults, using a structured data collection tool.The data was entered and analyzed using Jamovi software version 2.6.26. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression was performed to examine associations between sociodemographic variables and the knowledge and attitude for communicable diseases, reproductive health, and mental health services. The results are represented as unadjusted odds ratio and adjusted odds ratio with 95% confidence intervals. Results The study found that, overall, 58% of respondents exhibited poor knowledge as well as unfavourable attitudes toward utilising healthcare services. The study revealed limited knowledge among tribal people regarding healthcare services, with scores of 62.2% for communicable diseases, 71.9% for reproductive health, and 50% for mental health. Additionally, attitudes toward these domains were largely unfavourable, measured at 50.2%, 54.8%, and 60.5%, respectively. These outcomes showed a statistically significant association with demographic variables, including head-of-household status, age, religion, family size, educational attainment, and residence (p < 0.05). Conclusions PVTG community in Udupi district of South Karnataka, India, lack knowledge and favourable attitude towards healthcare services on communicable diseases, reproductive health and mental health. The findings underscore the urgent need for tailored health literacy initiatives and follow-up interventions among this PVTG to improve their health beliefs, and health status.

records.title: Work in a world in transition: disruptive facts and alternative paradigms toward a new world order
records.abstract: Abstract In this article, Santos M. Ruesga develops a structural analysis of contemporary transformations in the global economy, focusing on their implications for labor markets and institutional configurations. The article situates current dynamics within a context of overlapping disruptions—namely accelerated technological change (digitalization and automation), reconfiguration of global value chains, demographic transitions, and ecological constraints—arguing that these processes jointly undermine the explanatory and normative capacity of standard neoclassical labor frameworks. The author identifies key stylized facts, including labor market dualization, the expansion of non-standard and platform-mediated employment, declining labor share in income, and increasing heterogeneity in productivity and wages. These trends are interpreted through a political economy lens that emphasizes power asymmetries, institutional erosion, and the decoupling between productivity growth and employment quality. Ruesga advances the need for alternative analytical paradigms integrating insights from institutional economics, post-Keynesian approaches, and socio-economic theory. In this framework, labor is conceptualized not merely as a factor of production but as a socially embedded process shaped by regulatory regimes and collective actors. The article further explores policy implications, advocating for the redesign of welfare states, labor regulation, and income distribution mechanisms to address systemic precarity and inequality under conditions of structural uncertainty. The contribution concludes by framing the current conjuncture as a transition toward a redefined global socio-economic order, requiring new governance architectures capable of reconciling efficiency, equity, and sustainability in the organization of work.

records.title: Classroom Management Strategies and Their Impact on the Behavior and Academic Performance of Intermediate Pupils
records.venue: International Journal of Sustainability and Advanced Integrated Research
records.abstract: This study examined the impact of classroom management strategies on the behavior and academic performance of intermediate pupils at Tomas Claudio Colleges during the School Year 2025–2026. The study employed a descriptive survey research design complemented by documentary analysis. The respondents consisted of 247 intermediate pupils selected through total population sampling. A researcher-made questionnaire was utilized to assess the perceived impact of classroom management strategies on pupils' behavior in terms of emotional regulation, self-efficacy, and social skills, while documentary analysis of pupils' average grades was conducted to determine their academic performance. Descriptive and inferential statistical tools were used in analyzing the data. Findings revealed that most respondents were female, first- or second-born, belonged to families with two children, had a monthly family income of ₱50,000 and above, had parents who were predominantly college graduates, and whose parents were mostly government employees. Classroom management strategies were perceived to have a high impact on pupils' emotional regulation, self-efficacy, and social skills. Significant differences in these perceived impacts were found when respondents were grouped according to monthly family income, parents' educational attainment, and parents' occupation, while no significant differences were observed based on sex, sibling position, and family size. The respondents obtained a Very Satisfactory level of academic performance. Furthermore, a significant positive relationship was established between classroom management strategies and pupils' behavior and academic performance. The study concluded that effective classroom management strategies contribute to the development of positive behavioral outcomes and improved academic achievement among intermediate pupils. It is recommended that school administrators and teachers strengthen evidence-based classroom management practices through continuous professional development, foster home-school collaboration, integrate activities that enhance emotional regulation, self-efficacy, and social skills, implement the proposed action plan, and conduct further studies incorporating additional variables to broaden the findings.

records.title: Nation-Building: Hierarchies, Inequalities and Social Cleavages
records.abstract: Abstract This chapter examines how India pursues nation-building amid caste, tribal, gender, religious, and linguistic cleavages through democracy, federalism, and constitutionally embedded affirmative action, distinctive postcolonial institutional design. It details policies toward Dalits and tribals through anti-discrimination law, reservations, land reform, education expansion, forest conflicts, displacement, insurgency, bureaucratic neglect, violent backlash, and uneven administrative redress. The chapter analyzes Other Backward Castes politics by showing how the state creates prized government employment, intensifying distributional conflict, dominant caste assertion, and competitive identity mobilization across regions of generations. It evaluates women’s subordination alongside legal reform, political quotas, welfare schemes, educational gains, declining fertility, weak labor participation, rising agency, persistent son preference, and the marginalization of Muslims. Finally, the chapter assesses religion, language, federalism, migration, war, media, education, cinema, radio, television, smartphones, in forging cognitive unity while warning that majoritarianism and centralization threaten India’s plural democracy.

records.title: Effects of Nutritional Status on the Well-Being and Academic Performance of Grade Five Pupils
records.venue: International Journal of Sustainability and Advanced Integrated Research
records.abstract: This study examined the effects of nutritional status on the well-being and academic performance of Grade Five pupils in selected public elementary schools in Tanay District during the School Year 2025–2026. It employed a descriptive survey research design complemented by documentary analysis. The respondents consisted of 40 Grade Five teachers and 300 Grade Five pupils selected using Slovin’s formula. Data were gathered through a researcher-made questionnaire assessing the perceived effects of nutritional status on pupils’ physical, emotional, social, and intellectual development, while pupils’ academic performance was determined through documentary analysis of their average grades. Findings revealed that teachers perceived nutritional status to have a very high effect on pupils’ well-being across all developmental domains, whereas pupils rated its effect as high. A significant difference existed between the perceptions of teachers and pupils regarding the effects of nutritional status. Teachers’ perceptions did not significantly differ according to their demographic profile. Among pupils, no significant differences were found based on sex, sibling position, and family size; however, significant differences were observed in terms of monthly family income, parents’ educational attainment, and parents’ occupation. The pupils obtained a Very Satisfactory level of academic performance, and a significant relationship was established between the perceived effects of nutritional status on well-being and academic performance. The study concluded that nutritional status plays a significant role in pupils’ holistic well-being and is positively associated with academic achievement. It further established that socioeconomic factors influence pupils’ perceptions of the effects of nutritional status, while teachers’ demographic characteristics do not. The study recommends the continuous implementation and strengthening of school-based nutrition education programs, the provision of targeted academic intervention activities by teachers, the adoption of the proposed action plan, and the conduct of experimental studies to further examine the causal effects of nutritional status on pupils’ well-being and academic performance..

records.title: Building a Quality Culture in the Embryology Laboratory: The Role of Processes, Training, and Knowledge Exchange
records.abstract: Within the framework of the research project, a comprehensive analysis was conducted of the mechanisms through which a quality culture is formed and reproduced in contemporary embryology laboratories. The text consistently traces the evolution of managerial logic—from predominantly procedural quality control toward an integrated safety culture grounded in corrective and preventive action (CAPA) methodology, structured analysis of “near-miss” events (near-miss reporting), and continuous staff competency development as an essential condition for process reliability. Particular emphasis is placed on the deployment of technological solutions that reshape the architecture of laboratory practice: Piezo-ICSI, automation of “day-0” procedures, and the use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools for standardized assessment of morphological parameters of gametes and embryos. Drawing on provisions of international consensus documents (Vienna Consensus) and a body of studies from 2024–2025, it is shown that coupling high-technology production loops with standardized certification programs (ESHRE) reduces the contribution of the human factor while simultaneously increasing cumulative live birth rate.

records.title: Socio-demographic determinants of infant mortality among the Gond tribe in Satna district, Madhya Pradesh, India
records.venue: International Journal of Statistics and Applied Mathematics
records.abstract: Infant mortality is a key indicator of maternal and infant health and reflects the socio-economic and healthcare conditions of a community. Despite considerable progress in reducing infant mortality in India, tribal populations continue to experience disproportionately high infant deaths due to poverty, low educational attainment, inadequate healthcare services, poor sanitation, malnutrition, and limited access to maternal and infant healthcare. The present study aimed to examine the socio-demographic determinants of infant mortality among the Gond tribe in Satna District, Madhya Pradesh, India.A community-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 421 Gond households selected through a sampling technique. Data on live births were collected using a structured household interview schedule. The study assessed the influence of maternal and paternal education, household economic status, family size, occupation, maternal age at first birth, fertility behaviour, and women's participation in household decision-making on infant mortality. Descriptive statistics, percentage analysis, Pearson's correlation coefficient, and Student's t-test were used for data analysis. A total of 26 infant deaths were recorded among 821 live births. Infant mortality was higher among households with low parental education, poor socio-economic status, larger family size, early maternal age at first childbirth, and higher fertility. Mothers with greater participation in household decision-making experienced lower infant mortality than those with limited autonomy. A significant positive association was observed between the number of pregnancies and infant mortality. The findings indicate that socio-demographic factors play a significant role in determining infant survival among the Gond tribe. Strengthening maternal and child healthcare services, improving female education, promoting family planning, delaying the age at first childbirth, and enhancing women's decision-making autonomy are essential for reducing infant mortality and improving infant survival in tribal communities.

records.title: From the Scarcity to the Positive Abundance System: Solar Energy, Automation, and the Self-Domestication of Humankind as Drivers of a Transition to a Post-Capitalist Post-Scarcity Society
records.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
records.abstract: This working paper develops an integrated forecasting model for the transition of human societies from a scarcity system to a positive abundance system. Its starting point is that solar electricity follows a stable learning curve and is already the cheapest form of power generation. From near-zero-cost energy the paper derives - via automation, AI and closed material cycles - a decline of the marginal costs of key goods towards zero, so that money loses its function as the manager of scarcity. Three dynamics commonly read as threats are shown to be self-limiting: superfluous positional consumption, the population explosion (via the demographic transition), and interpersonal violence (primarily as a cultural civilising process; a genetic self-domestication component is treated as an uncertain, subordinate supplement). The favourable dynamics hold only within three boundary conditions - planetary boundaries, control over the orchestrating AI, and geopolitical justice between world regions - and raise inner questions of meaning, justice and macroeconomic stability. The technical transition appears largely determined over 80-120 years; what remains open and normative is solely its distribution - peaceful or contested. The paper closes with a framework for action (five guiding principles and 17 sequenced steps for global organizations, states and communities). A German-language version is included in this record. Version note (v6, 24 August 2026): This version revises the treatment oflearning rates. Assumption A1 now follows Lafond et al. (2018) and states theexperience-curve forecast as a distribution rather than a point estimate.Assumption A4 explicitly disclaims a learning-curve extrapolation from energyto goods, and a new limitation (L2) records that learning rates vary widelyacross product classes and are, for most goods, not statisticallydistinguishable from zero - so that H1 may hold while H2 fails. The bookscarry the same correction in their appendix.

records.title: The Confucian Fertility Paradox: Education Competition and Ultra-Low Fertility in East Asia
records.abstract: Total fertility rates in East Asia have fallen to levels without historical precedent, even though the region's Confucian heritage long placed extraordinary emphasis on family continuity and large families.We argue that this "Confucian Fertility Paradox" dissolves once we separate two strands of the tradition and recognize that modernization affected them very differently.The pro-natal strand, built on lineage continuity, ancestor worship, and reliance on sons for old-age support, was gradually switched off as child mortality fell, incomes rose, women entered the labor force, and state pensions replaced the family as the main source of security in old age.What survived was the second strand: the veneration of education and of status won through examination success, rooted in the imperial examination tradition.Under modern conditions this surviving strand reverses sign with respect to its effect on fertility.Where the historical examination system rewarded having many sons so that one might succeed, the modern single-ranking tournament rewards concentrating resources on one or two intensively educated children, and the quantity-quality tradeoff turns a once pro-natal culture into a powerful engine of low fertility.Drawing on recent empirical evidence from China and Korea, we show how education competition becomes the channel through which traditional values now suppress childbearing.We explain why standard pro-natalist policies, such as removing birth restrictions or offering cash subsidies, accomplish little when the underlying problem is a competitive equilibrium in parental investment, and we argue that policies aimed at the source of the distortion, such as structural reform of educational pathways, hold more promise.
