Government colleges losing students in Andhra Pradesh: A policy analysis
records.venue: International Journal of Political Science and Governance
records.abstract: Government colleges and universities in Andhra Pradesh have experienced a steady decline in student enrolment due to structural, demographic, and policy changes in the higher education sector. This study examines the impact of private higher education expansion, fee reimbursement policies, and slowing population growth on enrolment patterns in public institutions. Using secondary data from the All India Survey on Higher Education (AISHE), the University Grants Commission (UGC), the Andhra Pradesh State Council of Higher Education (APSCHE), and the Census of India, the study finds that private institutions account for more than 85% of higher education enrolment in the state, while government institutions enrol less than 15% of students. Fee reimbursement schemes have increased students' access to private colleges, and declining fertility has reduced the pool of college-age youth. The study concludes that improving academic quality, infrastructure, faculty strength, employability, and funding policies is essential for revitalizing government higher education institutions and ensuring their long-term sustainability.

records.title: Socioeconomic and Behavioural Determinants of Social Disconnectedness: Evidence from India
Assessment of sperm morphology in bulls, rams and humans: Classification systems, standardisation, and the application of machine learning
records.abstract: Sperm morphology is a critical predictor of fertility across a range of species; however, its assessment remains inherently subjective and thus susceptible to variability and inaccuracy. Morphological abnormalities can present in diverse forms, with over 25 distinct categories recognised in the current literature. These abnormalities may arise during spermatogenesis due to stressors, as well as post-maturation during epididymal storage, ejaculation, or as a consequence of suboptimal handling during processing. Researchers have long sought to characterise these abnormalities through classification systems. Numerous classification frameworks have been developed to categorise observed defects. However, inconsistencies in the classification of specific abnormalities have led to disputes among experts. Preferences for particular classification schemes vary among laboratories, species, industries, and geographic regions, resulting in a lack of standardisation that hampers comparability and contributes to considerable inter- and intra-observer variability. While advancements in automation have begun to emerge, subjective visual assessment remains the predominant method of evaluation. This reliance, combined with inconsistent classification standards, absence of formal training, and inherent human bias, continues to drive substantial variability. In response, recent research has turned to novel technologies such as machine learning to achieve objective, scalable assessment. However, training these models necessitates high-quality training data -something difficult to obtain given the challenges of standardising subjective assessments. To preserve the utility of sperm morphology as a useful indicator of fertility, it is essential that future efforts focus on improving assessor training and standardisation protocols, thereby reducing variability while the development of automated, objective technologies continues to progress.

records.title: Climate variability and fertility preferences in Zimbabwe: Examining the impact of environmental stress on the ideal number of children
records.abstract: Climate variability is increasingly emerging as an important determinant of demographic behavior, particularly in Agrarian societies where livelihoods remain highly dependent on environmental stability. While fertility transition scholarship has traditionally emphasized socio-economic factors such as education, urbanization, and marital change, limited empirical attention has been given to how climate stress shapes fertility preferences in Sub-Saharan Africa. Guided by Risk Society Theory and Life Course Theory, this study examines the relationship between climate variability and the ideal number of children in Zimbabwe, conceptualizing fertility preferences as socially embedded and environmentally mediated decisions shaped by both structural transitions and ecological uncertainty. The study uses nationally representative georeferenced data from the 2015 Zimbabwe Demographic and Health Survey linked with high resolution datasets from WorldClim and NASA Earth observation sources. A quantitative cross-sectional design was employed, and Poisson regression was used to model the count nature of the dependent variable. The analytical sample consisted of 9910 respondents. The Findings show that Mean temperature is positively and significantly associated with ideal family size (β=0.019, p<0.001), suggesting that rising temperature may reinforce pronatalist preferences in climate vulnerable contexts. Annual precipitation showed a weak positive association (β=0.002, p<0.093), while other climatic indicators were not statistically significant. Among socio-demographic factors, higher educational attainment significantly reduced fertility preferences, with tertiary education showing strongest negative effect (β=-0.435, p<0.001). Urban residence was associated with lower ideal family size (β=-0.0122, p<0.001), while marital union, age and household composition significantly increased fertility preferences. The findings suggest that fertility preferences in Zimbabwe are shaped not only by socio-economic transitions but also environmental uncertainty. The study contributes to climate demography by demonstrating that climate change climate change is becoming increasingly embedded in reproductive decision making and highlights the need to integrate reproductive health into climate adaptation policies.

records.title: The Global Transition – The Impact of Demographics and AI on Economic Power
records.abstract: The study uses a multi-region, dynamic life-cycle general equilibrium model covering more than 150 countries and 99% of the world's population to examine how demographic change will shape global development through 2100.The model incorporates three labor skill groups, internationally mobile capital, automation and AI adoption, country-specific fiscal policies and productivity growth, uncertain lifespans, and UN projections for fertility, mortality, and migration.Comparing the UN's 2017 and 2024 demographic projections reveals substantial global aging and a capital glut that drives long-run real returns very low.The more pessimistic 2024 forecast, particularly for Chinese fertility, reduces projected 2100 global GDP by 10% and sharply alters economic power: China's projected share of world GDP falls from 25.6% to 14.9%, while the US share rises from 11.2%to 14.4%.Results are highly sensitive to demographics and technology.Eliminating future US immigration reduces its 2100 global GDP share to 9.2%, while the UN low-fertility scenario cuts world output by roughly one-third.Faster automation and AI adoption further favors the technologically advantaged US.Under transformative AI and 2024 demographics, the US reaches 25.3% of global GDP in 2100 versus China's 16.9%, as internationally mobile capital increasingly flows toward superior technology.

records.title: Compulsory Schooling Mitigates Health Inequality: Anthropometric Evidence from Two Centuries of Height Data
records.abstract: Although compulsory education (CE) laws have widened access to schooling and shaped economic, social, and health outcomes, it remains unclear whether they reduce long-run health inequalities. We study the effect of CE policies on health inequality using height Gini indices for 66 countries between 1810 and 2000, estimating intent-to-treat effects through a staggered difference-in-differences design. Our results indicate that CE exposure reduces the height Gini. The inequality-reducing effect appears to operate mainly through increased years of schooling and reduced fertility. The effect is not uniform across regions, being largest in Europe, and it is driven largely by later extensions of CE duration rather than initial adoption alone. Overall, the findings indicate that education policy can meaningfully narrow health disparities over time, but its effectiveness depends on the scale of the mandate and the timing of adoption.

records.title: The status and influencing factors of pressure on women of childbearing age to have a child again: A cross-sectional study in China
records.abstract: Background Persistently low fertility and rapid population aging have increased concern regarding subsequent childbearing in China. Although fertility intentions have been widely examined, the multidimensional pressure experienced by parous women when considering another child remains insufficiently understood. Methods An online cross-sectional survey was conducted from January to June 2025 among 2097 parous women aged 18–49 years across 21 provinces and four municipalities in China. Subsequent fertility pressure was assessed using a validated 24-item scale. Guided by Becker's quantity-quality trade-off theory and the socio-ecological framework, hierarchical multiple linear regression was conducted by entering variables in four blocks: demographic characteristics, family and caregiving factors, socioeconomic and structural factors, and psychological and cultural factors. Results The mean subsequent fertility pressure score was 118.17 ± 23.41, indicating that women experienced pressure across multiple economic, occupational, health, childcare, child-development, and family-relationship domains. Higher fertility pressure was associated with poorer self-rated health, having more existing children, maternal primary caregiving, the absence of affordable childcare, lower personal and household income, smaller housing area, lower self-perceived social status, lower subjective wellbeing, more frequent Internet use, a lower ideal number of children, and weaker endorsement of lineage continuation. Compared with government-provided childcare, market-based childcare was also associated with higher pressure. Greater partner participation in housework and having only daughters rather than only sons were associated with lower pressure. The final model explained 26.3% of the variance in fertility pressure (Adjusted R 2 = 0.253). Conclusions Subsequent fertility pressure among parous women is a socially embedded experience shaped by physical capacity, cumulative caregiving demands, gendered household labor, material security, childcare provision, psychological resources, and fertility values. Policies should prioritize stable and affordable public childcare, a sustained redistribution of unpaid care through father-specific leave and paternal involvement, targeted economic and housing assistance, maternal health and mental health support, and protection of women's reproductive autonomy.

records.title: MAPPING GENOMIC VARIANTS ASSOCIATED WITH FUNCTIONAL AND HEALTH TRAITS IN DAIRY CATTLE POPULATION
records.venue: Archivio Istituzionale della Ricerca (Universita Degli Studi Di Milano)
records.abstract: This thesis aimed to integrate high-resolution genomic data with longitudinal phenotypes collected through Automatic Milking Systems (AMS).The objective was to investigate genetic variability, resilience, and udder health in Holstein dairy cattle.By combining genomic tools, sensor-derived time series, and veterinary treatment records, the study provides a multidimensional view of animal functionality under real farming conditions.The first chapter, "Genetic variability in dairy cattle", studied the genetic diversity of Holsteins bred in seven dairy farms in the Lombardy region through Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNP), Runs of Homozygosity (ROH) and Copy Number Variants (CNVs).The results revealed that intensive selection for milk yield, applied to Holstein cattle during the first decades of the 20th century, strongly shaped the genome of the breed.This process reduced variability in some regions while increasing the frequency of alleles linked to production.CNVs overlapping with genes involved in immunity and fertility suggested a role in adaptation.Within this chapter, these findings were presented in two published articles, providing the genetic background of the animals under study.The second chapter, "Resilience", addressed resilience using daily AMS data and statistical models to estimate expected lactation curves and calculate resilience indicators.Four indicators were evaluated: variance of milk yield deviations (LnVar), autocorrelation of residuals (rauto), frequency of perturbations (wfPert), and total milk loss (dPert).Analysis of nearly 600,000 daily records showed that older cows displayed greater variability and more frequent perturbations, while the capacity to recover (rauto) remained constant.Genome-wide analyses based on these indicators identified genes related to immune function, metabolism, and tissue integrity, confirming the complex biological nature of resilience.The third chapter, presented as a dedicated article, explores a novel approach that integrates AMS-derived perturbations with veterinary treatment records, thereby incorporating health information into resilience phenotyping.Deviations in milk yield were quantified as perturbation events described by duration, slopes of decline and recovery, and area of loss.Cows were classified into immunological susceptibility groups according to the temporal relationship between veterinary treatments and perturbations.This classification revealed clear differences in resilience indicators across categories.By aligning perturbation profiles with treatment timing (before, during, or after perturbations), the study showed that interventions significantly influenced both the severity of production losses and the trajectories of recovery.The fourth chapter, "Mastitis susceptibility/resistance in Holstein cows", focused on one of the more expensive diseases in dairy farming.Somatic cell count (SCC) and antibiotic treatments were used as a unique phenotype to map QTL linked to mastitis resistance, highlighting genomic regions associated with immune response and udder integrity.By combining SCC data with antibiotic treatments, the study provided a more comprehensive understanding of susceptibility and resistance to mastitis.Overall, this thesis demonstrates that resilience can be assessed in practice using AMS-derived phenotypes, reflects a partly poligenic genetic basis, and shows a close association with health events.The integration of genomic information with longitudinal data allow to identify animals that not only achieve high productivity but also cope better with stress and recover more quickly, with important implications for reducing antibiotic use, improving animal welfare, and enhancing the sustainability of dairy farming.In summary, the results show that combining genomic tools such as SNP, CNVs, and ROH with dynamic phenotypes derived from AMS provides new opportunities to select cows that are productive, healthy, and resilient.Alla vita e alle sue sfide, che sanno insegnare più dei successi.Ai baci e agli abbracci che hanno tolto peso ai giorni più difficili, alle risate che hanno reso più leggeri i pensieri, ai "sei brava, credo in te" che hanno fatto la differenza.Alla resilienza e al coraggio di cambiare strada quando serve.Holsteins, ROH reflect the story of demographic history and reveal the genomic footprints left by strong selection for production traits (Cortes-Hernández et al., 2022; Forutan et al., 2018).The length of ROH provides insight into the timing of inbreeding events: short segments typically reflect ancient common ancestry that occurred many tens of generations ago, whereas long ROH (>10-16 Mb) are signatures of recent inbreeding within the last 3-5 generations (Curik et al., 2014; Peripolli et al., 2017).Moreover, clusters of ROH, called ROH islands, are often found in regions containing genes important for milk yield, fertility, and disease resistance (Biscarini et al., 2016; Hajihosseinlo et al., 2023).Analyses in local breeds, such as the Aosta cattle, ROH have been used to characterize genomic variability and inbreeding, providing insights into demographic processes (Bernini et al., 2023).Taken together, SNP, CNV, and ROH give us complementary ways to describe genetic variability.SNP are the standard tool for genomic selection and association studies, CNV capture structural diversity linked to adaptation, and ROH provide insight into the distribution of inbreeding and past selection.Furthermore, the integration of these high-resolution genomic data allows for the identification of genomic regions under selection, including those associated with beneficial production traits and those contributing to the erosion of genetic diversity.This leads to a deeper understanding of the genetic architecture underlying complex traits and the dynamic interplay between selection pressures and genetic variation within the Holstein population.While genomic tools describe population structure and selection signatures, daily sensor data provide the dynamic, individual-level phenotypes needed to connect genetic variation with functional responses under different farm conditions. Precision livestock farming and the rise of longitudinal phenotypingOver the last two decades, livestock farming has increasingly integrated technological innovation and data-driven approaches to improve efficiency, animal welfare, and environmental sustainability.Within this context, Precision Livestock Farming (PLF) has emerged as a strategic framework that combines sensor technologies, automation, and real-time data analytics to monitor and manage animals at the individual level (Berckmans, 2017).Together with genomic resources, PLF enables a multidimensional characterization of each animal, supporting both real-time management and longterm breeding goals (Brito et al., 2020).PLF enables a transition from management based on population-level averages and intermittent farm visits, toward continuous, automated, and individualized livestock management.In the dairy sector, PLF has been notably driven by the widespread adoption of Automatic Milking Systems (AMS) and wearable sensors that collect highfrequency data on a wide range of parameters, including milk yield, milking speed, rumination activity, feeding behavior, and somatic cell count (SCC).These systems generate large amount of proactive promotion of resilience, integrating long-term genetic progress with real-time decisionmaking on farms.

records.title: From the Scarcity to the Positive Abundance System: Solar Energy, Automation, and the Self-Domestication of Humankind as Drivers of a Transition to a Post-Capitalist Post-Scarcity Society
records.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
records.abstract: This working paper develops an integrated forecasting model for the transition of human societies from a scarcity system to a positive abundance system. Its starting point is that solar electricity follows a stable learning curve and is already the cheapest form of power generation. From near-zero-cost energy the paper derives - via automation, AI and closed material cycles - a decline of the marginal costs of key goods towards zero, so that money loses its function as the manager of scarcity. Three dynamics commonly read as threats are shown to be self-limiting: superfluous positional consumption, the population explosion (via the demographic transition), and interpersonal violence (primarily as a cultural civilising process; a genetic self-domestication component is treated as an uncertain, subordinate supplement). The favourable dynamics hold only within three boundary conditions - planetary boundaries, control over the orchestrating AI, and geopolitical justice between world regions - and raise inner questions of meaning, justice and macroeconomic stability. The technical transition appears largely determined over 80-120 years; what remains open and normative is solely its distribution - peaceful or contested. The paper closes with a framework for action (five guiding principles and 17 sequenced steps for global organizations, states and communities). A German-language version is included in this record. Version note (v6, 24 August 2026): This version revises the treatment oflearning rates. Assumption A1 now follows Lafond et al. (2018) and states theexperience-curve forecast as a distribution rather than a point estimate.Assumption A4 explicitly disclaims a learning-curve extrapolation from energyto goods, and a new limitation (L2) records that learning rates vary widelyacross product classes and are, for most goods, not statisticallydistinguishable from zero - so that H1 may hold while H2 fails. The bookscarry the same correction in their appendix.

records.title: Formal Agricultural Credit Access among Paddy Farmers in Tripura: Distribution, Dependency and Determinants
records.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
records.abstract: The study explores and examines the access, distribution, dependency and determinants of formal agricultural credit among paddy cultivators in selected villages of Tripura. The study is based on primary data collected from 370 paddy cultivating farm households across eight selected villages of Sepahijala and South Tripura districts of Tripura. This research work analyses the distribution of borrowers and formal agriculture credit across villages and farm size categories and assesses farmers\\\' dependency on formal credit. The findings suggest recognisable variation informal credit access across villages and farm sizes. The study further identifies and confirms the factors influencing access to formal credit using Binary Probit Model. The explanatory variables incorporate landholding patterns, asset ownership, irrigation status, educational attainment, caste status, HYV cultivation, age, family size and household labour availability. The probability of accessing formal credit is significantly influenced by the farmers\\\' productive resources, agriculture intensity, human capital and household characteristics, derived from the results. The findings show the existence of variations in formal credit access and emphasize the need for more inclusive and accessible agriculture credit availability in the study area.

records.title: Education, care, and fertility in South Korea: essays on household constraints and social pressure
records.abstract: This dissertation studies how family decisions about education, care, and fertility are shaped by social pressure and household constraints. Across the three chapters, I focus especially on South Korea, where very low fertility has coincided with intense educational competition, high private education spending, and persistent gendered expectations around childcare. The dissertation combines empirical evidence and theoretical modeling to examine how peer behavior, parental time allocation, and education-related status competition can raise the perceived cost of children and contribute to lower fertility. The first chapter, "Can Parents Overspend in their Children's Education? Peer Effects in Korea's Shadow Education Market,'' studies peer effects in household tutoring expenditures using the Korean Education Longitudinal Study. I focus on the transition from middle school to high school, when students in many equalization areas were assigned to general academic high schools by district lottery and re-sorted into new schools and peer groups. The results show that peer exposure affects household tutoring spending, with the clearest increases occurring when students enter the top quartile of the peer-spending distribution. More moderate upward moves produce weaker and less stable effects, while downward transitions are associated with sharper reductions in spending. These findings suggest that high-spending peer environments can intensify positional pressure and shape household education investment in Korea's shadow education market. The second chapter, "How Many Parents Does It Take? Parental Time Allocation and the Effectiveness of Fertility Subsidies," develops an overlapping-generations model of parental childcare time, fertility, and human capital investment. The chapter asks whether greater paternal involvement necessarily reduces mothers' childcare burden. When maternal and paternal time are substitutes, father involvement can relax the maternal time constraint. When they are complements, however, greater father involvement can raise mothers' childcare time as well, lowering fertility and shifting resources toward child quality. The chapter also shows that fertility subsidies may have limited or unintended effects when they do not change the underlying organization of care. The third chapter, "Rat Race, Educational Signaling, and Fertility," develops a model linking peer pressure in education spending to fertility and long-run demographic outcomes. Households choose consumption, fertility, and shadow education investment, but perceived child quality depends partly on spending relative to peers. This creates overinvestment in education and lowers fertility. The chapter then embeds this mechanism in a dynamic framework in which population and human capital evolve jointly. Calibrating the model to Korea suggests that shadow-education competition creates a modest but meaningful fertility distortion and contributes to excessive education spending.

records.title: The Economics of Human Shrinkage
records.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
records.abstract: 1. Objective This study investigates the socio-economic determinants driving the global contraction in Total Fertility Rates (TFR) below replacement levels ($\approx 2.1$) using a longitudinal global panel spanning 1990 to 2024. 2. Methodology & Execution Microeconomic Formalization: Formulated a structural framework extending Becker’s Quantity-Quality Trade-off model and maternal time opportunity costs. Panel Econometrics: Compiled 6,120 country-year observations via the World Bank API, estimating Pooled OLS, Panel Fixed Effects (FE), and Two-Way Fixed Effects (TWFE) models with Driscoll-Kraay robust standard errors. Diagnostic Auditing: Conducted Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) diagnostic checks to eliminate multicollinearity distortions across demographic proxies. 3. Key Findings & Impact The Income Paradox Reversal: Discovered a major econometric divergence: while cross-sectional Pooled OLS displays a negative relationship between income and fertility ($\beta = -0.089^{}$), isolating within-country variation over time via Panel Fixed Effects reveals a positive pro-natalist liquidity effect ($\beta = 0.097^{***}$). Opportunity Costs & Urbanization: Confirmed that urbanization ($\beta = -0.0251, p < 0.001$) and female labor participation structurally depress TFR by increasing child-rearing maintenance costs and career opportunity costs. Infant Mortality Core: Identified infant mortality reduction as the single strongest historical catalyst driving modern family rationalization and fertility contraction ($\beta = 0.0162, p < 0.001$).

records.title: Essays on the Microeconomics of Immigrant Fertility Assimilation
records.abstract: Summary Despite being a fertile field for testing and further developing theoretical economic models of fertility change, the empirical immigrant fertility literature has remained mostly isolated from theoretical models of fertility in economics. Unlike fertility transitions that take place over generations, immigrant fertility assimilation, which is the tendency of immigrants to move away from their native fertility norms toward those of their host country, is as common an occurrence as immigration itself. Different immigrant groups show different levels of fertility assimilation at any point in time. This high level of frequency and variation makes it a candidate for empirical research aimed at hypotheses and model testing. Fertility decision making is one of the topics that showcased the potential explanatory power of classical microeconomic models of the household beyond what is considered clas- sical “economic” decision making. Economic theories of fertility model a decision making process that social scientists traditionally did not deem to be of an economic nature. By mod- eling children as a commodity that can be assigned a price in the household’s optimization problem, it was shown that a classical model of the household can generate results in line with empirical observations. One of the major breakthroughs in that area was the successful work by Gary Becker, in which he developed a framework to theoretically explain the fertility transition towards lower fertility in developed countries by exploring the quantity-quality trade-off in fer- tility decision making, where fertility outcomes are not only measured by quantity—the number of children—but also by the quality of children—education and health, among other criteria. The model successfully demonstrated how a household’s optimal fertility changes when market parameters, such as income and prices, change. This cumulative dissertation consists of five essays with the aim of opening a channel between established microeconomic fertility theories and the immigrant fertility literature. A the- oretical component demonstrates how classical models of fertility in microeconomics can be used to motivate empirical hypotheses. To showcase this potential, the analysis focuses on so- cial interaction with natives and learning as a mechanism that can generate testable empirical hypotheses when integrated into a theoretical framework. Social interaction in general has been the focus of increased theoretical and empirical investigation in economics. Specifically in the area of fertility, social interaction plays an important role in shaping fertility culture. Although the immigrant fertility literature identifies factors that overlap with social interaction as drivers of fertility assimilation, such as education and language proficiency, this is, to my knowledge, the first attempt to link immigrant fertility assimilation and social interaction with natives, whether theoretically or empirically. Data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP) are used to test the association between immigrants’ social interaction with natives, measured by the incidence of home visits, and fertility assimilation. Primary data from a survey experi- ment are then used to test for the effect of learning on the propensity for fertility assimilation among Pakistani students preparing for emigration. The survey is further used to explore the underlying nature of fertility decision making by examining the exact factors the Pakistani students consider relevant for their fertility decision making in the context of their planned em- igration. Particularly, they are asked to state whether they consider economic factors the most relevant or base their fertility decisions on cultural concepts such as identity, family pressure, and family expectations. This, in turn, serves as further exploration of the nature of the under- lying mechanism of a potential association between social interaction with natives and fertility assimilation. Such an association can be a result of information transmission that informs im- migrants’ economic fertility decision making or simply a mechanism of societal pressure from having natives in immigrants’ immediate social network. The stated beliefs of the respondents offer insight into which of the two mechanisms is more likely to generate the association in question. The first essay introduces a fertility assimilation model based on social interaction with na- tives. The essay demonstrates how extending a classical quantity-quality model of fertility by embedding a Bayesian learning mechanism can generate results that resemble immigrant fertility assimilation. The model assumes that immigrants have biased information about the price structure of the quantity and quality of children, where the cost of quantity is the commodity cost per child, which is assumed to be observable, and the cost of quality comprises expendi- tures such as education and healthcare. The quality costs of children are strongly influenced by the institutions of the host country, about which immigrants do not have perfect information. Through social interaction with natives, who possess superior knowledge about host-country institutions, immigrants are capable of updating their beliefs about the host-country-specific price of quality. It follows from the model that a higher exposure to natives through social interaction leads to a posterior belief about the price of quality that is more in line with the natives’ beliefs, and thus to fertility assimilation. The exercise shows the unused potential of mathematical economic models to provide insight into contemporary fertility behavior. The second essay is an empirical investigation motivated by the theoretical framework. Using data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP), I find that the incidence of immi- grants engaging in home visits with natives is strongly correlated with fertility assimilation. In a sample restricted to first-generation immigrants from high-fertility countries, I find that the interaction through home visits is linked to a decrease in completed fertility by up to 56 chil- dren per 100 immigrants. A similar significant correlation is not reproducible using a placebo variable that measures visits to friends. Language proficiency, despite showing a similar posi- tive correlation with fertility assimilation, does not eliminate the significant association shown by home visits. An alternative independent variable measuring the strength of the sense of Ger- man identity among immigrants is used to test the hypothesis that mutual visits with natives are an indicator of cultural change in terms of propensity to integrate or a changed identity. It does not show a similar significant association. In the third essay, Bernd Hayo and I explore the nature of the underlying mechanism of fertility decision making, and eventually fertility assimilation, among immigrants. We use pri- mary data from the Survey on Fertility Plans and Attitudes among Pakistani University Students Preparing for Emigration. The survey collects stated preferences that directly relate to the theo- retical hypothesis discussed earlier. Concretely, the participants are asked about the factors that are relevant for shaping their fertility in general and also factors that are likely to drive them to change their fertility plans after emigration. The survey includes an experimental component where a treatment group is exposed to a statement indicating that immigrants tend to assimilate their fertility to that of their host country. We find that respondents consider economic factors to be the main factors that would affect their fertility decision making in general and also in the context of emigration. They give less weight to non-economic factors such as identity and social influence from the family, favoring factors that resemble economic modeling of fertil- ity over others closer to behavioral theories. Moreover, the treatment group shows a higher propensity for fertility assimilation, indicating that potential immigrants are willing to update their beliefs and fertility plans based on information made available to them. This hints at the potential relevance of a learning mechanism as described in the first essay. The fourth essay documents the Survey on Fertility Plans and Attitudes among Pakistani University Students Preparing for Emigration. It includes general information about the sam- ple and sample design, and the complete questionnaire in English and in Urdu—the original language in which the questionnaire was administered. Additionally, the distributions of all variables are presented in tabular form. In the fifth essay, I look at fertility preferences and beliefs of German and Pakistani youth from a comparative perspective. I identify variables in the SOEP and in our survey from Pak- istan that document respondents’ beliefs about the ideal number of children and the factors that affect their fertility decision making. While different answer scales and differences in the framing of questions prevent me from performing statistical analysis, I visually inspect the dis- tributions to form an impression of whether the core underlying logic behind fertility beliefs and intentions is different across cultures. I find suggestive evidence that respondents from both samples agree that mainly economic factors and constraints shape their fertility plans.

Key Findings & Impact The Income Paradox Reversal: Discovered a major econometric divergence: while cross-sectional Pooled OLS displays a negative relationship between income and fertility ($\beta = -0.089^{}$), isolating within-country variation over time via Panel Fixed Effects reveals a positive pro-natalist liquidity effect ($\beta = 0.097^{***}$). Opportunity Costs & Urbanization: Confirmed that urbanization ($\beta = -0.0251, p < 0.001$) and female labor participation structurally depress TFR by increasing child-rearing maintenance costs and career opportunity costs. Infant Mortality Core: Identified infant mortality reduction as the single strongest historical catalyst driving modern family rationalization and fertility contraction ($\beta = 0.0162, p < 0.001$).

records.title: スライダブルホイールを有する全方向移動ロボットの軌道追従制御および機構開発
records.abstract: Background and motivation.In recent decades, societies across the globe, particularly in Japan, Europe, and increasingly in China and other parts of Asia, are facing a profound demographic shift characterized by declining birth rates, shrinking working-age populations, and rapid aging.This demographic transition has led to chronic labor shortages in sectors that rely heavily on physical work, such as manufacturing, transportation, retail, and eldercare.In response, there is an urgent and growing demand for automation technologies that can supplement or replace human labor in routine, repetitive, or physically demanding tasks.Mobile robots have emerged as a key enabler of this automation wave and are already widely deployed for material transportation in factories and warehouses, where they enhance operational efficiency while reducing labor costs.However, the demand for automation is no longer limited to highly structured industrial environments.In retail settings, such as supermarkets and convenience stores, tasks including shelf restocking, customer guidance are increasingly being targeted for robotic implementation.Similarly, in last-mile delivery and indoor service applications, mobile platforms are being integrated with robotic manipulators or humanoid upper bodies to create versatile, multi-functional service agents.For such applications, the mobile base must support agile navigation through dynamic, crowded, and spatially constrained indoor environments.In this context, omnidirectional mobile robots offer significant advantages over conventional differential-drive counterparts.Unlike differential-drive robots, which require rotational maneuvers to reorient before lateral movement, an omnidirectional platform can instantaneously translate in any direction.This capability enables seamless navigation through narrow aisles, rapid obstacle avoidance, and precise alignment with shelves, counters, or interaction points, all without the need for additional maneuvering space.Consequently, omnidirectional mobility is not merely a performance enhancement but a critical enabler for effective operation in complex human-centric environments.Omnidirectional mobile robots can be roughly divided based on the moving parts into four types: wheeled robots [1-8], legged robots [9-12], wheel-legged robots [13-15], and tracked robot [16,17].Wheeled omnidirectional mobile robots are the most common because of their low energy consumption, simple structure, and high stability.The non-holonomic constraints of conventional wheeled mobile robots can be removed with mechanisms such as Omni wheels [18,19], Mecanum wheels [20,21], caster wheels [22][23][24][25], and spherical wheels [26][27][28][29][30].

The impact of family planning policy on the intergenerational transmission of education: evidence from China’s one-child policy
records.abstract: This paper examines the effect of China’s One-Child Policy (OCP) on intergenerational transmission of education (ITE) by exploiting its staggered rollout across provinces as a quasi-natural experiment. We find that exposure to the OCP significantly increased the persistence of education across generations, thereby reducing intergenerational mobility. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that this effect is driven primarily by the Han ethnic group—the policy’s primary target—whereas no significant change is observed among exempt ethnic minorities. Furthermore, we show that stricter local enforcement of the policy led to a stronger parent-child education correlation. We rationalize these findings with a quantity-quality trade‑off model, where the exogenous fertility constraint raises per-child educational investment among better-educated parents. This study establishes that population policies can have profound and unintended consequences for the intergenerational transmission of advantage, extending inequality research to family planning and offering a framework for assessing the social equity implications of future demographic interventions.

records.title: Back To School: The Effects Of Re-Entry Policies On Teen Mothers' Education In Senegal
records.abstract: This study examines the effect of Senegal's 2007 school re-entry circular on women's educational attainment. Prior to 2007, pregnancy resulted in permanent expulsion from school in Senegal; the 2007 circular replaced this with a re-entry process, allowing a pregnant student to return to school after childbirth upon presenting a medical certificate. Pregnancy remains one of the leading causes of girls' school dropout in Sub-Saharan Africa, and despite the widespread adoption of re-entry policies across the region, there is limited causal evidence on whether they improve educational attainment. This study uses a difference-in-differences design, exploiting variation in exposure to the 2007 policy by respondents' sex and birth cohort, using pooled Senegal Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) data from 2008–2023. Because the policy targeted girls whose schooling was interrupted by pregnancy, women constitute the policy-eligible group, while men who were exposed to a related 2004 compulsory schooling law but not to the re-entry provision serve as a comparison group. We expect that exposure to the re-entry policy increased women's completed years of schooling and school completion rates relative to men's, with larger effects for cohorts more fully exposed to the policy. The study also examines secondary outcomes including literacy, employment, marital, and fertility outcomes.

Historical, Demographic, Economic, and Social Data: The United States, 1790-2002
records.abstract: This data collection contains detailed county and state-level ecological and descriptive data for the United States for the years 1790 to 2002. Parts 1-43 are an update to HISTORICAL, DEMOGRAPHIC, ECONOMIC, AND SOCIAL DATA: THE UNITED STATES, 1790-1970 (ICPSR 0003). Parts 1-41 contain data from the 1790-1970 censuses. They include extensive information about the social and political character of the United States, including a breakdown of population by state, race, nationality, number of families, size of the family, births, deaths, marriages, occupation, religion, and general economic condition. Parts 42 and 43 contain data from the 1840 and 1870 Censuses of Manufacturing, respectively. These files include information about the number of persons employed in various industries and the quantities of different types of manufactured products. Parts 44-50 provide county-level data from the United States Census of Agriculture for 1840 to 1900. They also include the state and national totals for the variables. The files provide data about the number, types, and prices of various agricultural products. Parts 51-57 contain data on religious bodies and church membership for 1906, 1916, 1926, 1936, and 1952, respectively. Parts 58-69 consist of data from the CITY DATA BOOKS for 1944, 1948, 1952, 1956, 1962, 1967, 1972, 1977, 1983, 1988, 1994, and 2000, respectively. These files contain information about population, climate, housing units, hotels, birth and death rates, school enrollment and education expenditures, employment in various industries, and city government finances. Parts 70-81 consist of data from the COUNTY DATA BOOKS for 1947, 1949, 1952, 1956, 1962, 1967, 1972, 1977, 1983, 1988, 1994, and 2000, respectively. These files include information about population, employment, housing, agriculture, manufacturing, retail, services, trade, banking, Social Security, local governments, school enrollment, hospitals, crime, and income. Parts 82-84 contain data from USA COUNTIES 1998. Due to the large number of variables from this source, the data were divided into into three separate data files. Data include information on population, vital statistics, school enrollment, educational attainment, Social Security, labor force, personal income, poverty, housing, trade, farms, ancestry, commercial banks, and transfer payments. Parts 85-106 provide data from the United States Census of Agriculture for 1910 to 2002. They provide data about the amount, types, and prices of various agricultural products. Also, these datasets contain extensive information on the amount, expenses, sales, values, and production of farms and machinery.

records.title: THREE ESSAYS ON PUBLIC POLICIES AND INEQUALITY IN CHINA
records.abstract: This dissertation contains three essays examining three influential public policies in China and their various outcomes over the last half-century. The first essay examines the quantity–quality trade-off induced by China's family control policy during the 1970s. Using two waves of Chinese census data, I find China's “Later, Longer, Fewer” policy from the 1970s significantly reduced fertility in the country. The second essay measures and examines the earning gaps among local urban workers and migrant workers using the 2002 China Household Income Project (CHIP2002) survey data. Relative to the urban workers, this study finds negative earning differentials and lower education returns among migrant workers. The third essay investigates the impacts of railway expansion in China on the urban-rural income gap over the last three decades. Using provincial panel data through a DID framework shows a positive relationship between railway expansion and improved urban-rural income inequality.

records.title: 博物館のサテライト化による理科・環境学習
records.abstract: It has been reported that the number of children who hate studying science has increased over the last decade or more. Accourding to the TIMSS2007 survey, a part of score and ranking according to country went up. It was estimared from this that decline in academic achievement stopped in Japan. However, bipolarization is looked at by the interest of science in a choolchid. Moreover, as for the junior high school student, greediness for learning did not necessarily go up. It was already clear from OECD's PISA2006 report that the proportion of responses such as, "I am interested in science and curious about it." and "I feel that science is fun. "among students completing their compulsory education in Japan is at a low level internationally. With this background in mind, the Lake Biwa Museum has advanced a satellite museum program in the schools of Shiga Prefecture, involving the use of actual specimens on site and science studies led by museum curators. As a result, many children developed a curiosity towards science learning and became eager to learn programs voluntarily that were concerned with their own natural surroundings. In addition, the number of children who were interested in the preservation of the natural environment increased along with development of a positive attitude towards such tasks as the cleaning of neighborhood ponds and rivers.

records.title: 1 Under Pressure? The Effect of Peers on Outcomes of Young Adults
records.abstract: A variety of public campaigns, including the “Just Say No ” campaign of the 1980s and 1990s that encouraged teenagers to “Just Say No to Drugs”, are based on the premise that teenagers are very susceptible to peer influences. Despite this, very little is known about the effect of school peers on the long-run outcomes of teenagers. This is primarily due to two factors: the absence of information on peers merged with long-run outcomes of individuals and, equally important, the difficulty of separately identifying the role of peers. This paper uses data on the population of Norway and idiosyncratic variation in cohort composition within schools to examine the role of peer composition in 9th grade on longer-run outcomes such as IQ scores at age 18, teenage childbearing, post-compulsory schooling educational track, adult labor market status, and earnings. We find that outcomes are influenced by the proportion of females in the grade, and these effects differ for men and women. Other peer variables (average age, average mother’s education) have little impact on the outcomes of teenagers.

records.title: Free lower secondary education and gendered labour market consequences: Evidence from Ghana
records.venue: OpenSALDRU Publications Repository (University of Cape Town)
records.abstract: Following substantial progress towards universal primary education, governments have increasingly shifted attention to reducing barriers at the secondary school level. Tertiary education participation remains rare across Sub-Saharan Africa, meaning secondary school is increasingly the final stage of education most young people will complete before entering the labour market. In this paper, we study the labour market consequences of Ghana’s Free Compulsory Universal Basic Education (1996), a component of which removed fees at the lower secondary level. Using a difference-in-differences design based on treatment intensity and birth-cohort exposure, we estimate the effects of the reform on forms of economic (in)activity, disaggregated by gender. We find that the reform raised educational attainment: scaled by the 10th-90th percentile range of the observed dose, the average causal response implies years of education rose by roughly a quarter of a year, junior high school completion by 2.8 percentage points and literacy by 4.6 percentage points. In the labour market, the reform bolstered employment in the districts where it had most scope to operate, and did so along different margins for men and women. Men’s participation in any productive activity was unchanged while employment for pay or profit rose (3.5 percentage points) and production for own final use fell (2.9 percentage points) – a movement across the ICLS-19 production boundary. This occurred alongside a 2.5 percentage point gain in skilled occupations and a 2.4 percentage point gain in public sector employment. Women also left own-use production, by 3.9 percentage points, but only about three quarters of that exit entered employment: the remainder moving out of work and into care/family responsibilities. Women’s employment gain was almost wholly informal and vulnerable, with wage employment and skilled work falling. Demographic evidence suggests that part of women’s withdrawal reflects the timing of childbearing rather than a permanent change in labour supply.

records.title: Awareness And Involvement of Parents to School Activities in Relation to the Learners' Academic Performance
records.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
records.abstract: This study determined the level of parents’ awareness and extent of involvement in school activities in relation to learners’ academic performance. Respondents were grouped according to age, family size, highest educational attainment, average family monthly income, and grade level. Parental awareness was assessed in terms of curricular and non-curricular activities, while parental involvement was examined across parenting, communicating, volunteering, learning at home, decision-making, and collaborating with the community. The study also assessed learners’ academic performance during the first and second quarters and examined significant differences and relationships among the variables. The respondents were parents of Grade 6 and Grade 10 learners at St. Sebastian International School-Neg. Occ., Inc., Bacolod City, and data were gathered using a modified parental involvement questionnaire by Alderete. Findings revealed that parental involvement in communicating significantly differed by age, while volunteering showed no significant differences across all demographic variables. In learning at home, a significant difference was found only by grade level. Decision-making significantly differed by age, while collaborating with the community significantly differed by age and educational attainment. No significant relationship was found between parents’ awareness and learners’ academic performance. However, parental involvement was found to have a significant relationship with learners’ academic performance, indicating that greater parental involvement in school-related activities is associated with improved academic outcomes.
